It is published as a single volume alongside the *Akulavīratantra*, the *Kulānandatantra*, and the *Jñānakārikā*. The printed volume also includes introductory material and summaries in English.

The first chapter, the Determination of the Knowledge of the Kula:
the tip of the nail of the big toe of the root [channel]— these are the continuous succession of the principles (tattva).
O Goddess, knowledge within the sphere of the Kula is of eighteen kinds.
O Bhairavī, I have explained the union of emanation exactly as it is;
O Lord, what else do you ask? That which is most secret has been made manifest.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Jñānanirṇītīyoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and emerged from Candradvīpa. 1/1.
The second chapter. The Goddess said:
"The penance of the five fires was performed for many tens of millions of years."
O Bhairava, by your grace, may that penance of mine today be perfected.
The yoga of creation has been understood by me; now tell me about the yoga of dissolution.
Bhairava said: "Excellent! I shall explain to you how the withdrawal (saṃhāra) occurs;
that which is known as Kālāgnirudra is eternally situated at the tips of the nails. (2.2)
When it blazes upward, it is then the state of withdrawal;
and its greatness as the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) is established suddenly in the netherworld (Pātāla). // 2.3 //
The seven netherworlds (pātālas) have been described, and above them, heaven is situated;
these, O auspicious lady, are declared to be the fourteen worlds.
O Dear One, she who exists in the form of the *tattva* within the center of the body is to be known;
[therein] all-knowledge is dissolved, and dissolution occurs within the sphere of power (*śakti*). (2.5)
The Śakti has entered into the midst of Śiva; Śiva abides in the midst of Kriyā (action).
Within Jñāna (knowledge), Kriyā is dissolved; by His will, Kriyā dissolves away.
O beautiful one, I have described to you this process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) in its distinct divisions, wherein the power of will (icchā-śakti) dissolves into that supreme Śiva who is light (tejas).
When the steps are placed in the mode of withdrawal, he who is wrathful withdraws the universe;
when the steps are placed in the mode of creation, he thus creates the world of moving and non-moving beings.
O fair-faced one, enjoyment is established below and liberation is above;
O Goddess, that which was previously indicated by me to you as the yoga of emanation (sṛṣṭiyoga), [is this]. 2.9.
The foundation of Kula has been described according to the principle of emanation and reabsorption.
O Lord, what else do you ask? That which was most secret has been made manifest. (2.10)
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Jñānanirṇītiryoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and emerged from Candradvīpa. 2/2.
The third chapter. The Goddess said:
O Maheśāna, [please explain] the characteristic of the Kula, preceded by self-awareness.
This is my doubt, O Lord; be gracious, O Śaṅkara.
Bhairava said:
Listen with one-pointed mind; the definition of the Kula is being declared.
Wherever the sight is, there the mind is, as well as the elements, the senses, and the individual soul (pudgala). 3/2
The vision, which is the life-force of one’s own power, has reached dissolution through hundreds of thousands [of repetitions].
The fourfold [practice] consists of the place, the meditation, the color, and the number of repetitions. (3.3)
The perception of a mass is the locus; that state is called meditation.
Color and form are pointed out, yet the characteristic is indeed devoid of form. (3.4)
O fair-faced goddess, the aggregate (piṇḍa) consists of both the manifest form and that which transcends form;
O Goddess, it resides in various locations, being fourfold for each one.
O fair-faced one, [there are wheels] with four petals, eight spokes, and twelve spokes;
O beloved, [there are also those] with five spokes, sixteen spokes, and sixty-four petals.

Above that, there is a hundred-petaled lotus, richly endowed with beauty, adorned with a thousand petals; then a ten-million-petaled lotus, abounding in great splendor—listen further to what follows. (3.7)
Endowed with thirty-five million [petals], provided with three crores [of others], and likewise shining, it is joined with pericarp and filaments. (3.8)
Above that is the all-pervading, eternally risen, and indivisible Sovereignty (svātantrya);
it is the lotus, immovable, all-encompassing, and stainless. (3.9)
By His will, creation comes into being, and therein it goes to its dissolution;
for that reason it is renowned as the *liṅga*, wherein the moving and the unmoving are dissolved (*līna*). (3.10)
Bondage is declared to be the failure to know the form that is an unbroken circle, changeless, and partless; by knowing it, one is liberated from all bonds. (3.11)
Free from the states of mind with or without the *manas*, devoid of meditation and concentration, it is eternally and always directly perceptible, resembling a blue lotus. (3.12)
O Goddess, this God consists of all castes yet is devoid of all castes;
he is attainable through knowledge, O Goddess, and has come down through the succession of the lineage. (3.13)
O Goddess, it has been declared that the likeness of the Kula-mark remains as such;
[it is] neither a linga made of wood nor one made of clay, nor one produced from stone or precious gems. (3.14)
The mind is not made of brass and the like, nor of gold produced from iron; it is not crystal, nor even lead, nor tin, nor born of copper. (3.15)
Those [sciences] originating from emeralds and others honored by the world, the eighteen worldly treatises, as well as those concerning the cruel and the spiritual; 3/16.
O Goddess, one should not even mentally worship that which has been worshipped by them;
what is the reason for this, O Mahādevī? Because they are like cattle, devoid of knowledge. (3.17)
Those who are ignorant, of evil conduct, and devoid of the family precepts—no association with them should be enjoyed, nor should one accumulate wealth from them. (3/18)
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Asuras rich in asceticism,
the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas, and even the grasses, shrubs, and ants— 3/19.

The planets, constellations, stars, and so forth—the entire world of the stationary and the moving—have emerged within the center of the *bindu*; having become one in the state of *līlā*, they are identical with it. (3.20)
The creator of creation and destruction, that liṅga worshipped by the Siddhas—vibrant, stainless, eternal, immeasurable, and ever-arisen. (3.21)
Blazing like a meteor, with the brilliance of lightning in the firmament—having recognized and beheld this supreme liṅga, one becomes a vessel for liberation. (3.22)
The Liṅga shall not be destroyed by masses of stone-rain from most terrible great clouds, nor shall it fall when struck by a thunderbolt. (3.23)
O Goddess, one who desires spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) should worship this Kaulika;
he should honor him with mental flowers, fragrant incenses, and radiant lamps. (3.24)
Non-violence is the first flower; the second is the restraint of the senses; the third is the flower of compassion, and the fourth is the flower of pure intention. (3.25)
The fifth is the flower of forbearance, the sixth is the conquest over anger;
the seventh is the flower of meditative concentration, and the eighth is the flower of wisdom. (3.26)
Having understood this procedure for flowers, one should worship the mental liṅga;
indeed, by worshipping the body-liṅga, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

O Goddess, this mark of accomplishment (siddhiliṅga), residing within the body and accompanied by signs of realization, is the mark of the mind; one should always meditate upon it for the attainment of whatever fruit one desires. (3.28)
They attain that, without a doubt, preceded by self-realization;
this, O Goddess, is the characteristic of the Kaulika-dehaliṅga for you. (3/29)
O Goddess, one who has attained the path should avoid any other [image] made of stone, wood, or clay; such worldly [images] are devoid of both spiritual perfection and liberation. (3.30)
In the Kula tradition, only he whose latent impressions (vāsanā) reside within the body possesses a share [in liberation];
he whose latent impressions reside outside is a bound soul (paśu), colored by the physical body. (3/31)
Thus, O Goddess, this definitive exposition of knowledge has been told to you by name;
it should be given to one endowed with devotion, but it must not be given to one devoid of devotion. (3.32)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Jñānanirṇitīyoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and originating from Candradvīpa. || 3/3 ||
The Fourth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, today my birth has become fruitful; penance has been well-performed by me."
O Bhairava, by your grace, my body has become stainless today.
When the paralysis of the fetters occurs in one's own home or in one's own country, [one may perform] restraint and favor, as well as transference and abduction. (4.2)
Even while conversing with an image and shattering pots and stones, how is it that you alone have become my refuge through the complete withdrawal of all things? (4.3)
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! O you of great austerity, I shall explain it:
having inscribed the *kulapiṇḍa* together with the channels and the openings of the channels."
The auspicious *piṇḍa*, consisting of knowledge and mantra, bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
it is [visualized] through the openings of the channels, both above and below, illuminated by the letter *ra*.
Vāyuviṣṇu, together with the bindu, has the luster of molten gold;
he is absorbed within the circle of birth, possessing a radiance equal to both darkness and light. (4.6)

O auspicious lady, the practitioner, by means of the moving and non-moving [beings], effects the paralysis of the hands and other such feats within the heart of the body of the victim, as well as within the body of the sacrificial animal. (4.7)
Likewise, there is the Bindu, the Nāda, and the Śakti, as well as the meditation on the radiant [light];
it is dissolved within the maṇḍala of birth, possessing a luster equal to darkness and light. (4.8)
Having visualized [the deity] as residing within the body of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), the bound soul (paśu) is praised for half a moment;
then, having meditated upon the Power (śakti) in the form of a flash of lightning within the five voids (vyomapañcaka).
And in half a ghaṭikā, O fair-faced one of great mind, the entire world is shaken by the piercing of the knowledge of Śakti through the [power] called Manas.
Having bound even the mountains with this noose, one should cause them to tremble;
having attacked the supreme power in the body of another by means of the resonance (nāda), one should pierce it.
Whether walking, sitting, or while forming mudrās, when questioned, she will speak of both the past and the future. (4.12)
O Bhairavī, from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*, O beloved, is the knowledge of the conch-consecration for the mass of the Kula, beginning with the tooth-stick and so forth. (4.13)

O Dear One, each [mantra] is illuminated by its respective syllable, consisting of a handful of flowers, a hand-stroke, and the rites of killing, driving away, paralyzing, deluding, and so forth. (4.14)
O Dear One, having understood the combination of the fifty syllables, perform all rites—whether pacifying, prospering, nourishing, attracting, or subjugating. (4.15)
HŪṂ is killing; YŪṂ YAḤ is eradication; RŪṂ RA is causing fever; BUṂ VA is driving away; LŪṂ LA is paralyzing; ŚŪṂ ŚA is pacifying; ṢŪṂ ṢA is pinning down; KṢEṂ KṢA is...;
KṢUṂ KṢA is seizing cattle; KLĪṂ KṢṆĪṂ is subjugation; KLEṂ KṢṆOṂ.

*Soṃ saḥ* is agitation and delusion; *sadyapratyayaḥ* is the accomplishment (*siddhi*). *Ho haḥ* is the destruction of poison. *Hro hraḥ* is the attraction of blood and of Yoginīs. *Jūṃ saḥ* is the conqueror of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*). ... [It effects] speaking to and the bursting open of images and the like. *Sroṃ śaḥ* is the paralysis of bonds (*pāśastobha*) and so forth, the fuel for the form of desire (*kāmarūpindha*), *bhrū tra*.
Ḍākinīsiddhi; jhura, Rākṣasīsiddhi; lūṃ la, Lākinīsiddhi; luṃ ka, Kusumālinīsiddhi; yūṃ ya, Yoginīsiddhi; hrīṃ ha, Ākarṣaṇa (attraction).
But by means of each individual seed-syllable, one should differentiate the mass of phonemes; O Goddess, it performs the action that is desired by the mind. (4.16)

In the rites of initiation and the concluding sacrifices, one should employ the Mātṛkā in reverse; having understood everything, one who possesses firm concentration should join that [Mātṛkā] to the foundation of the Kula. (4.17)
The bound soul (paśu) should establish that supreme liṅga, which is merged within the form of radiant energy;
thus, being autonomous, he attains liberation in the abode of the heart of all.
"Bhairava has spoken thus: 'O auspicious lady, that which you have asked is the cause of success, though it is most secret; it is the perfection of all-knowing qualities. (4.19)
It must be guarded with great effort from the wicked who lack devotion;
it should not be given to one devoid of devotion, even if they desire the Kaulika accomplishment. (4.20)
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Jñānanirṇītiyoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and emerged from Candradvīpa. 4/4.
The Fifth Chapter. The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, out of your grace, please tell me of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Just as delusion, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, comes to an end.
Speak, O Mahādeva, of that supreme [teaching] which utterly destroys delusion.
Bhairava said:
By that very knowledge alone and through the constant practice of meditation,
one becomes liberated from all dualities and remains intent upon the state beyond practice.
One shall accomplish all goals as desired by the mind; arise! [There is] the sword, the netherworld, the yellow pigment, the collyrium, and the sandals. (5.3)
O Goddess, there shall be the pill, flight through the sky, mercury, and the elixir;
there shall be invisibility, as well as other elixirs. 5/4.
She shall accomplish it; of this there is no doubt, provided she remains joined with meditation on the state [of the deity].
Listen with a single-pointed mind, O beloved, as it is being told by me. 5/5.
White, cool, divine, fragrant, and of great splendor, it was a celestial object bringing moon-like delight, approaching from the midst of the sky. (5.6)
By means of the many-holed [nostril], that which flows forth will soon conquer death;
for him there is neither old age nor death, and no affliction of disease exists. (5.7)
O fair-faced one, by such play he indeed becomes a possessor of supernatural powers;
[he beholds] the white expanse of lotuses situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
Or, the wise one [should visualize] himself in the center of that [lotus] which has a thousand times ten million petals, seated right there and adorned with white ornaments. (5.9)
O beloved, one should visualize that very same lotus as being covered from above by all the finest portions of the Ocean of Milk, while it is being sprinkled [with those waters]. (5.10)
They are liberated from all diseases and from the bonds of old age and death;
they sport with various enjoyments and are born in whatever form they desire. || 5/11 ||
Now I shall further explain the specific method for conquering death:
having meditated upon [the deity] seated on a lunar throne and struck upward by the moon. (5.12)
One should visualize [the body] being sprinkled with divine, cool sprays of water, liberated from old age and death, and free from all diseases. (5.13)
Through practice for a year, one attains equality with the families of the Yoginīs;
and hear another marvel, O Goddess, you who are born of the Kula. (5.14)
O Goddess, by meditating upon this [form], which is like the orb of the moon when it is full, complete, and perfectly filled, old age and disease are destroyed. 5/15
Now listen to another [method], O auspicious one, according to its true nature, O noble lady:
one should meditate on this moon, O Goddess, as being at the navel, the head, and situated in the heart. (5.16)
One who possesses an even mind should practice this continuously for one year;
thereafter, he attains independence, freed from old age and death. (5.17)
I shall speak further; listen, O you who are honored by heroes!
It is richly adorned with a thousand petals and resembles the whiteness of cow’s milk. (5.18)
The wheel situated on the goddess's wheel is likewise positioned by the sky-farers;
it is mounted upon the lower wheel and flooded by the upper wheel. (5.19)
The yogi who practices constantly, being sprinkled with the special [nectars], becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair, and is liberated from all diseases. (5.20)
O beloved, he sports as far as the edge of the ocean and attains perfection through his own sovereignty;
O Goddess, listen with a one-pointed mind to another wonder as well. (5.21)
Having meditated upon that sixteen-petaled lotus, radiant like snow, jasmine, and the moon, in each of its locations, extending from Śiva down to the sphere of the Avīci hell. (5.22)
With the falling streams of drops, his body was filled with splashes;
and from the pores of his skin, [the nectar] emerged, resembling cow’s milk or snow. (5.23)
For him there is no old age or death, nor is there the affliction of disease;
independent and equal to Śiva, his movements and actions proceed according to his own will. (5.24)
She is worshipped in manifold ways by hosts of gods and divine maidens in the secret place, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the head, and within the crest-lock. (5.25)
O Goddess, situated at the joint of the crown, there is a triple-staff in the middle of the back;
O Goddess, the wheels are of eleven kinds and consist of a thousand [spokes]. 5/26.
It may have five spokes, eight petals, ten, twelve, sixteen, a hundred, or even ten million petals. (5.27)
When practiced thoroughly in these positions, O Goddess, it bestows various fruits; when red, it is always subjugating and grants great enjoyment. (5.28)
Yellow is always for causing paralysis, O Lord; smoky-grey is for driving away;
white is said to be for nourishment and specifically for bringing about pacification.
That which is white as a stream of cow's milk is said to be beneficial for the conquest of death;
that which has the luster of molten gold is the cause of the agitation of cities and the like. (5.30)

Having meditated separately upon the Bindu, the Nāda, and the Śakti in this manner, one attains virtue and wealth, pleasure and liberation, as well as the eightfold qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā). // 5.31 //
O Goddess, the transformation of form regarding the past and the future certainly occurs in this way for one who is devoted to that practice; of this there is no doubt. (5.32)
Devotion to the Guru [leads to] immortality for yoginīs within the Kulakaula scriptures; O Goddess, one shall conquer death, of this there is no doubt. (5.33)
O Goddess, the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], which is the definitive conclusion of all knowledge, has been told;
it must be guarded with effort in the world of mortals from the lowest of men. (5.34)
This collection of accomplishments, which is difficult to attain, must be guarded with great effort;
it should be given to one who has previously attained perfection after being tested for one year. (5.35)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, extracted from Candradvīpa, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda, in the Jñānanirṇītīyoginīkaula. 5/5.
The sixth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Kula, today my birth has become fruitful within my body."
O Lord of the Kaula, by your grace, I have understood the definitive teaching of the Kaula. (6.1)
I wish to know other things; tell me the characteristics of the living being (jīva).
Who is this that is designated as the jīva, or what is the essential nature of the jīva?
What is its color, what is its dimension, and in what place is it situated? Into what indeed does it dissolve? Tell me all of that. (6.3)
Bhairava said: Listen, O Vīracāmuṇḍā, to the excellent determination regarding the living soul;
it is supreme, partless, eternal, free from disease, and stainless.
The Lord is called the atom; he is Śiva, the all-pervading, the supreme. He who is the individual soul (jīva), the most transcendent, is the Haṃsa, the personification of Śakti. || 6/5 ||
He is the mind, He is the supreme vital breath, and He is indeed the intellect and the consciousness;
He is the wind that fills the air, residing within all living beings. (6.6)
As long as it remains within the body, it is called the individual soul (jīva);
the moment that body is abandoned, it is declared to be the Supreme Śiva. (6.7)
O Goddess, that which resides in the navel, the heart, the throat, as well as the mouth and nostrils, and that which resides in the ears, is heard through the lineage of successive transmission. 6.8
O Goddess, this Kaulika [teaching] has come from ear to ear;
O fair-faced one, by the mere knowledge of it and by its hearing, [one attains liberation]. 6.9
One who practices the saffron robe, free from bondage, for six months shall be liberated from all the sins accumulated by you. (6.10)
For him also, grief, mental anguish, old age, and disease are destroyed;
liberated from all maladies, he attains union with the yogis. (6.11)
The mastery of qualities such as *aṇimā* and the attainment of mental perfection shall arise;
this practice regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) has been taught to you, O Bhairavī. (6.12)

It should be given to one who is deeply devoted to the family lineage (kulāgama), who worships the Guru and the Goddess, who is endowed with all [proper] dispositions, and who is firm in resolve. (6.13)

The essential Kaula essence, which is the source of the Yoginīs, must not be given to one who is deceitful, fraudulent, cruel, or who merely wears the outward signs [of the path] through elaborate displays. (6.14)
The Goddess said: "O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, my ascetic penance has become fruitful today;
today my body, which was struck by the veil of ignorance, has become stainless. (6.15)
The great knowledge that has been revealed, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain—I now wish to hear about the auspicious method for deceiving Time. (6.16)
Bhairava said: "O Lord, I have now been asked by you about that which is exceedingly profound;
I shall explain it without doubt, how death is destroyed. (6.17)
Stretching out [his tongue] until it reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila),
even though his wise mind is being consumed by the tip of nectar with the tip of the essence.
"By practicing this for one month, O one of great austerity, one shall conquer death; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Having placed the breath at the root of the palate, one should drink [the vital air] slowly. (6.19)
O Goddess, by practicing for six months one is liberated from great diseases;
when practiced for one year, old age and death are destroyed. (6.20)
One hears even the past and the future, as well as sounds from afar;
furthermore, poison does not take effect in the body, even if one is bitten by great serpents. (6.21)
Whether it be stationary, moving, or even artificial poison, one who has attained that state is not cut down even when being cut, just as the mind is absorbed in that [object]. (6.22)
One should know that the nectar situated between the two [eyes] in the form of a drop (bindu) is the destroyer of wrinkles and graying hair. (6.23)
Having placed the tongue in the cool position of touch, the wise man becomes free from wrinkles and graying hair, and is liberated from all diseases. (6.24)
Death does not befall him who is always devoted to the vehicle of yoga;
he should apply the tongue to the root of the palate for the destruction of disease. (6.25)
Whether standing, waking, sleeping, walking, eating, or engaged in sexual union, one should constantly contract the tongue, keeping it joined with one's own palate. (6.26)
Death does not come to him; for a year he becomes one who moves according to his own will, having fixed the mind within the heart until it has attained the state of *unmanī*. (6.27)
O fair-faced one, one may destroy death that has arrived within half a ghaṭikā;
O Goddess, this deception of Time, which is most secret, has been revealed. (6.28)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇītīyoginīkaula*, brought down by the illustrious Śrī Śaghnapāda and originating from Candradvīpa. 6/6.
The seventh chapter. The Goddess said:
[Tell me] the knowledge for the stabilization of grey hair, which destroys old age and death.
O Lord, how did I come to take refuge in you alone, the triple reality? 7.1
Bhairava said:
O Vīramātṛ, listen to the knowledge for the stabilization of grey hair;
contemplate the Goddess as situated within the wheel, like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight. (7.2)
Cool and resembling the moon, the wick is ignited by ghee;
there, O fair-faced one, the flame is absorbed within the wheel of bones.
One should meditate upon collyrium located on the mass of hair, firmly attached, moist, and black in form; it destroys wrinkles and gray hair. (7.4)
O Goddess, listen now with a one-pointed mind to the second [method]: one should practice the cooling yoga in the location of the foundation and the trunk. (7.5)

One should indeed behold the sun, which is dissolved in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and consists of liquid black collyrium, as if it were an enemy; and the moon, likewise, as if it were a friend. (7.6)
Wearing black garments constantly, his soul colored by meditation on Kṛṣṇa, he should stay in an underground chamber in a secluded place free from gadflies and mosquitoes. (7.7)
Not in a place crowded with people, nor one devoid of snakes and tigers;
but in a secluded, solitary, divine spot, beautified by heaps of flowers. || 7/8 ||
Having perfumed it with fragrant incense, one who has conquered the senses with śāli rice will, within six months, attain accomplishment and become equal to the state of a Yoginī. (7.9)
O fair-faced one, this [mantra] is equal to Kāmadeva, is worshipped by celestial maidens, and resides within the Brahma-knot; these are indeed the three [aspects], O lovely-faced one. (7.10)

O Dear One, one should indeed dye with the liquid the entire [body], including the pores of the skin and so forth—which has the luster of crushed blue collyrium and resides within the Brahmakhaṇḍa. (7.11)
One whose self is colored by meditation becomes, even if old, possessed of exalted youth;
of this there is no doubt within six months. (7.12)
The sixteen-spoked wheel situated within the tawny knot is exceedingly radiant, accompanied by the vowel *ṛ*, black in color, and adorned with the sixteen vowels. (7.13)
Having moved upward from the point illuminated by the khadyota, they have reached dissolution in the *brahmarandhra*.
Through practice cultivated for six months, even an old man becomes like a youth. (7.14)
There is no doubt that he becomes like Kāmadeva with a second;
having resorted to the station of the Yoginīs, he is dark, of black complexion. (7.15)
Flowing from the eight petals, cool and resembling the moon, it rests upon the skull at the base of the hair; one should color it with its brilliance. (7.16)
Whether for half a year or even for a full year, though old, he appears as a youth of sixteen;
he is liberated from old age and death, and is entirely free from disease and ailment.
The common [energy] of the host of Yoginīs is the cause of creation and dissolution;
the radiance situated in the hollow of the throat has gone to its absorption in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (7.18)
It is like liquid collyrium flowing forth from the pores of the skin;
it is the hidden, structural bond of the very beauty of the bodiless god of love.
The hair of that person grows constantly upon his dense bones;
in the first [case], it is a thorn to people, while in the second, it is the destroyer of pain. (7.20)
In the third [birth], there is indeed the state of being a poet, charming with poetic ornaments; in the fourth, the power of speech; and in the fifth, the ability to hear from afar. (7.21)
The sixth [stage] is proclaimed as the piercing of the earth and the guest;
and in the seventh, the state of union with the Yoginīs certainly arises. (7.22)
O beloved Goddess, in the eighth [birth] you become the remover of old age;
in the ninth you possess fierce speed, and in the tenth you assume many forms.
Endowed with eleven qualities, peaceful, and free from the threefold [impurities], he is worshipped just like Śiva, being possessed of those same eleven qualities. (7.24)
One may perform ascension, description, and even dance at will; for one should go to that very place where the mind finds delight. (7.25)
When the Kaulika [teaching] has indeed been known, one should not restrain the mind;
for the scripture is free from conceptual proliferation, and the Guru is free from conceptual proliferation. (7.26)
The mantra is free from conceptual proliferation; Śiva is free from conceptual proliferation.
This, O Lord, is the Kaula tradition; the bound soul, O Dear One, is characterized by conceptual proliferation.
Having deceived themselves by those [deeds], they in turn deceive others;
some are ruined through ignorance, and some are ruined through negligence. (7.28)
Some are destroyed by the circle of knowledge, and some are destroyed by those who have perished;
likewise, there is trembling, paralysis, wrath, the mudrā, and leaping. (7.29)
There is no doubt in this matter: within seven nights during the Kaulava period, whatever he touches with his hand and whatever he beholds with his eye [becomes his]. (7.30)
All that becomes pure when struck by the rays of the supreme bindu;
this is called the knowledge of the stabilization of grey hair, O beloved of the Yoginīs. (7.31)

O Goddess of the gods, O Goddess Kāmakalā, this [practice] beginning with the wheel, which follows the path up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), is joined with the supreme stabilization of graying hair.
This secret has been told to you: the definitive realization of the knowledge of *unmanī*. (7.32)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, extracted from Candradvīpa, brought down by the venerable Śrīmacchaghna, in the Jñānanirṇitiyoginīkaula. 7/7.
The eighth chapter. The Goddess said:
O Lord, [this] is extremely profound, well-guarded, and the most excellent secret.
O Bhairava, how indeed has the deity Kula arisen within the Akula?
Whether born of the field (kṣetra), born of the seat (pīṭha), born of yoga, or born of mantra;
whether innate (sahaja) or born of the family (kula)—such is the sixty-fourfold [system]. || 8.2 ||
O Lord, tell me the procedure for the sequence of worship as established by the Kula tradition;
and tell me everything regarding the procedure for the worship of the Guru in brief. (8.3)
Bhairava said:
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Yoginī, Vīra, and Mātṛ!
[Practice] in a solitary, secluded place adorned with garlands of flowers. (8.4)
Having perfumed it well with incense, and provided with fish, meat, and [other delicacies], together with various kinds of food and drink, and accompanied by the joy of wine. || 8/5 ||
O Great Goddess, whether she is endowed with power, a high-born woman, one born of a noble family, or even one from the lowest caste—I shall now describe their distinct classifications. (8.6)
He whose marriage has been performed with one born of the same lineage is called a *sahaja*.
They say that one born of a noble family is a *vaiśyā*, while those of the lowest caste are *antyajāḥ*. (8.7)
O Goddess, the external [practice] has been explained; now hear the internal [practice], characterized by the bliss of passion through the application of the permissible and the impermissible. 8.8
O Beloved, that innate power (sahajā śakti) indeed dwells within the center of the body;
how could she, whose nature consists of the assembly of letters and the Kula, not be known as Kulajā? 8.9
O Dear One, it is said that [the power] residing in the body is threefold and that residing outside is also threefold.
O Goddess, listen as I explain the one born of the lowest [caste] exactly as it exists.
Resembling pure crystal, a garland of pearls, and the mistress of birds,
the Great Power (Mahāśakti) is perfectly purified in her upward and transverse directions by her own great splendor.
This is the high-souled Śakti Antyajā Vyomamālinī;
her mouth is filled with betel, and she is smeared with musk. 8.12.
With a mind full of joy and contentment, one should prepare two separate vessels for the yoginī and the vīra, containing sandalwood paste and musk respectively. 8.13.
One should worship those sixty-four [deities], as well as the fifty-eight;
all of them wear red garments and are radiant with armlets and bracelets.
One should worship the circle of Yoginīs and Heroes according to one's capacity;
such is the Kula-teacher presided over by the sons of the Kula. (8.15)
O fair-faced one, those born of the field (kṣetraja) who are established there should be worshipped by the Great Goddess, as well as Karavīra, Mahākāla, and Devikoṭya. (8.16)
Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Caritra, Ekāmraka,
as well as Aṭṭahāsa and Jayantī— by these sacred fields (kṣetra) are those born of the field (kṣetrajāḥ).
Among them, O beloved, those who are born in the preeminent [field] are the true kṣetrajās.
Hrīṃ śrīṃ hrī śrīṃ, the feet of Koṅkaṇā;
hrīṃ śrī hrī śrīṃ, the feet of Kalambā;
hrīṃ śrīṃ hrī śrīṃ, the feet of Nāgā.
Hrīṃ śrīṃ hrī śrīṃ, O feet of Harasiddhā!
Hrīṃ śrī hrīṃ śrīṃ, O feet of Kamvī!
Hrī śrī hrī śrī, O feet of Maṅgalā!
Hrīṃ Śrī Hrī Śrī Siddhā-īpāda;
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrī Śrī Vachā-īpāda;
Hrīṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Śrī Śivā-īpāda.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrī-Icchā-īpāda | Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ā-īpāda | Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrī Vīrā-īpāda |
Hrīṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Śrī, O you whose feet protect the three worlds! Hrīṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Śrī, O you who possess the form of Varāha!
Hrīṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Śrī, O you who are indeed the Kṛta Yuga!
Likewise, O Goddess of gods, she who is born in the field is worshipped for the attainment of perfection throughout the four ages—Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. (8.18)

O Goddess, one should first utter "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" at the end of the feet and likewise pronounce the name; thus the [mantras] born of the field (kṣetrajā) have been described. Now I shall tell you those born of the sacred seats (pīṭhajā). 8.19
O virtuous one, this seat named Kāmākhyā has arisen as the foremost;
it is the abode of the Siddhas for the seven goddesses situated in the Upapīṭhas. (8.20)
Furthermore, O Dear One, the second seat (pīṭha) is Saṃjñā Pūrṇagiri; [then there is] Oḍiyāna, the great seat (mahāpīṭha), together with its subsidiary seats (upapīṭha). 8.21.
The *pīṭha* is half of an *arvuda*, accompanied by an *upapīṭha*.

Listen, O beloved, to the procedure for the worship of the deities of the *pīṭhas* and so forth, including the collection of *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*, as well as the *kṣetras* and *upakṣetras*. (8.22)
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Mahālakṣmī;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Kusumānaṅgā;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Śuklā.
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, homage to the feet of Pralambā!
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, homage to the feet of Pulindā!
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, homage to the feet of Śavarā!
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Kṛṣṇāī;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Lacchāī;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Nandāī.
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the venerable feet of Bhadrā;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the venerable feet of Kalambā;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the venerable feet of Campā.
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Dhavalā;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Hiḍimbā;
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, the feet of Mahāmāyā.
O auspicious one, those excellent yoginīs who have been born in the multitude of pīṭhas and upapīṭhas—
when they are worshipped by these [means], all the Mothers attain accomplishment.
O Dear One, those who have attained perfection through the practice of yoga are born of yoga; those who have attained perfection through the propitiation of mantras are born of mantra. (8.24)
Together with their mothers and goddesses, those of great strength fought with roars;
they consumed the divine sacrificial pap (caru) and the animal destined for seven future births.
O Goddess of gods, those who have been conceived in their wombs and have consumed the exudation, as well as those born from the womb, come to know their own conception. (8.26)
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī with the thunderbolt in hand, and likewise Yogeśvarī. (8.27)
Aghoreśī is renowned as the Mother who is remembered as all-pervasive;
likewise, there are others who are guardians of the gates, by whom this entire world is pervaded. (8.28)
And in the sequence of the five births, one should always worship all those others everywhere—in cities and villages—as well as the Guru together with the Siddhas. (8.29)
The planets, the *nāgas*, the gods, the *yoginīs*, and the *siddhas*—
these honor her when she is honored, but they disregard her when she is insulted.
O Dear One, I shall now proclaim the eight *kulas* and the ritual procedure for the eight groups of eight.
Hrīḥ / Ā hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Iṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Ūṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Ṛṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Ḷṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Aiṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Oṃ hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / Aḥ hrīḥ. First, O Goddess, hear this eightfold Vidyā-mantra:
Hrīḥ / Kṣaḥ hrīḥ / Laḥ hrīḥ / Haḥ hrīḥ / Saḥ.
Hrīḥ ṣaḥ hrīḥ śaḥ hrīḥ va hrīḥ ra—this is declared as the eightfold sequence of the Vidyā. Hrīḥ kla hrīḥ—O Bhairavī, this is the Kaulika [Vidyā].
One should write the Vidyā in eight ways, differentiated by the first group of eight.
Just as this is so, so too should all [the others] be understood according to the sequence of the Yoginīs. (8.31)
According to the prescribed rule, there are eight groups of eight, totaling sixty-four in due order;
this is the wheel of the assembly of Yoginīs, possessing the eight qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. (8.32)
There is indeed no doubt that this occurs for one who is devoted to meditation and worship;
furthermore, the second great wheel is the activator of all types of attraction. (8.33)
The seizing of animals and the possession [of others] belong to one devoted to worship and meditation;
the third, however, is the great wheel of entering another's body. (8.34)
O beloved, through practice, one surely attains both the past and the future, as well as whatever various desired objects exist; of this there is no doubt. (8.35)
The fourth is the auspicious Peaceful Wheel, which bestows both liberation and further deliverance;
having worshipped this wheel, one applies oneself to meditation as long as necessary. (8.36)
In an instant, there occurs a paralysis [of the senses] through various types of mudrā-bindings;
and diverse forms of speech arise, both those never heard before and those already heard. (8.37)
This scripture consisting of limbs should be recited; the networks of mantras are heard.
It is heard by oneself from oneself, and within oneself by oneself. (8.38)
Within six months, O beloved of the Yoginīs, one attains perfection;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one becomes like a second Kāmadeva. (8.39)
The fifth, however, is the Great Wheel; by means of the sequence of meditation and worship, one destroys [the elements] beginning with wind through speech, and he remains like one who is mute. (8.40)
And the sixth is indeed the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), which bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
and the seventh wheel, O Goddess of Gods, is supreme for paralyzing armies.
The wheel of stimulation, possession, and so forth, which liberates one from the bonds of saṃsāra, is visible even from afar to one who is devoted to worship and meditation upon it. 8.42.
The eighth wheel is designated as that which sets in motion the accomplishment of one's desires;
O auspicious one, O beloved, it effects killing, expulsion, paralyzing, deluding, and so forth. (8.43)
Having understood the great wheel of speech that stands established through devotion to the family (kula), and its arrangement of eight times eight, one attains success; not otherwise. (8.44)
Thus, I have explained to you without doubt that secret essence of theirs, the sequence of the sixty-four Yoginīs; indeed, grasp it with devotion and through proper reasoning. (8.45)
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Jñānanirṇītīyoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and originating from Candradvīpa. 8/8.
The Ninth Chapter. Bhairava said:
O Sulocanā, I shall proclaim the lineage of gurus and the lineage of Siddhas.
O beloved, I shall now describe to you the arrangement of the lineage of Yoginīs.
[He is] Khecarī, the mother of all, among all the Siddhayoginīs;
[and he is] the entire sacred field (kṣetra) among all the Yoginīs who move on earth and whose range is everywhere. 9.2.

Those born from all mantras, those born from all yogas, those born from all sacred seats (pīṭhas), those born from all innate natures (sahajas), those born from all families (kulas), and all female gatekeepers. || 9.3 ||
Born from all wombs in the Kṛta, Dvāpara, Tretā, and Kali ages,
they are worshipped by the Yoginīs for the attainment of siddhi according to the division of the four yugas.
The supreme secret among secrets has been revealed to you through your devotion.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Kaulas, by your grace my body has been perfectly consumed by fire today and completely extinguished; I have realized the definitive conclusion of knowledge."
Now I wish to hear from my teachers about the worship of the Siddhas.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, you who possess the nature of the Kula, listen to the procedure for the attainment of the Guru:
[the lineage of] Śrī Viśvapāda, (Śrī) Vicitrapāda, and Śrī Śvetapāda.
To the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda; to the venerable Maheśvarapāda; to the venerable Bṛhadīṣapāda;

to the venerable Vindhyapāda; to the venerable Śabarapāda; to the venerable Mahendrapāda; to the venerable Candrapāda; to the venerable Hiḍinipāda; to the venerable Samudrapāda; to the venerable Lavaṇapāda; to the venerable Dumbarapāda.
To the feet of Śrī Deṇe; to the feet of Śrī Dhīvara; to the feet of Śrī Siṃhala;
to the feet of (Śrī) Oginī; to the Guru, Paramaguru, Parameṣṭhin, Pūjya, Mahāpūjya, Lākinī, Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Kākinī, and Yākinī.
Having placed the syllable *hrīṃ* at the beginning and the syllable *śrīṃ* immediately thereafter,
one should cause the arrangement of these two syllables to be bestowed upon the others at the end.
And the perfected ones and yoginīs are perfected in this Kula tradition;
there has never been, nor will there ever be again, a knowledge equal to this. (9.7)
In this most terrible Kali age, which is exceedingly fearsome like Raurava,
sixteen Siddhas have been born within this Kaula tradition, O fair-eyed one; whereas in the Kṛta,
Dvāpara, and Tretā ages, the Siddhas were honored by heroes.
I shall describe the procedure for their naming; listen, O lady of beautiful eyes. (9.8)
Those with feet like female deer; those with feet for descending; those with feet like the sun; those with radiant feet;
those with feet like lotuses; those with feet like tigers; those with feet like female antelopes; those with feet like peacocks; those with soft feet; those with feet like hanging bellies.
These were the great siddhas of old, the introducers of Kulakaula; O Lord of Gods, they are the impellers of the independent Kula throughout the four ages. (9/9)
By the power of his knowledge, many men attain perfection;
this Kaula tradition, originating from the Supreme, consists of ten crores [of verses]. 9/10.
O auspicious and beautiful lady, the Yoginī named Icchā is the most essential of the essential within the Great Kaula; she reaches the end of Māyā through the supreme will of the Siddhas. (9.11)
Furthermore, O Goddess, it was later revealed by their own will to the Khecarīs; and again, O Beloved, it was told to the Mothers by the Khecaras.
O Mistress of the Families, they shall go to the Mothers among the Bhūcarīs;
O Dear One, this has been declared regarding the Bhūcarīs who are excellent eaters. 9.13
Born into the lineage of the Yoginīs, one clearly attains the Kaulikī [state], whereas others are tormented within the eighty-four thousand matrices of the womb-machine (yoniyantreṣu). (9.14)
Afterwards, the meritorious soul, a marvel of his lineage, shall obtain this knowledge;
he will attain the great siddhis of enjoyment and liberation, and become beloved by the yoginīs. || 9/15 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, extracted from Candradvīpa and brought down by the illustrious Śrī Śaghnapāda, in the Great Kaula known as Jñānanirṇītiyoginī. 9/9.
The tenth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, today my very body has become fruitful for me."
With his body enveloped by fire, he stood poised upon a single foot.
O Bhairava, that penance of mine has become fruitful today through you who are pleased;
O Lord, the definitive conclusion regarding knowledge has been revealed to me this day. (10.2)
Again I ask, O Lord of Kaula; speak according to reality, O Master, so that the division into eight groups of eight may be thoroughly understood.
Even now, O Lord, there remains a doubt regarding those individual wheels (*cakras*).
O Bhairava, how is it that the secret place, like a wheel, is swiftly accomplished? 10.4.
"O Lord, the summary of their locations, meditations, and fruits is being told.
Bhairava said:
'Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! You have asked me about that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.'"
I shall speak without doubt, O fair-faced one, for you who are endowed with devotion:
*lāṃ līṃ lūṃ ḷṃ luṃ laiṃ lauṃ laḥ*; *hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ hṛṃ h haiṃ hauṃ (haḥ)*; *sāṃ sīṃ sūṃ sṛṃ slaṃ (saiṃ) sauṃ saḥ*; *ṣāṃ ṣīṃ ṣūṃ*.
Ṣṛṃ ṣlaṃ ṣaiṃ ṣauṃ ṣaḥ | Śāṃ śīṃ śūṃ śṛṃ ślaṃ śaiṃ śauṃ śaḥ | Vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vṛṃ vlaṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaḥ | Hlāṃ hlīṃ hluṃ hḷṃ hlaiṃ hlauṃ hlaḥ || 10 ||
The syllable *kṣa* is at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), while the syllable *laṃ* is on the two foreheads.
One should place the letter *ha* between the eyebrows, the letter *sa* in the circle of the face, the letter *ṣa* in the region of the throat, and the letter *śa* in the heart. (10.7)
The syllable *va* is in the center of the navel, while the syllable *hlā* is in the lotus-root;
these are declared to be the wheels of the locations (*sthānacakra*). Listen, O beloved, to their meditation (*dhyāna*). (10.8)
Resembling pure crystal, with upward-radiating, stainless brilliance,
it is a divine eight-petaled lotus adorned by the first group of eight.
Completely liberated from all dualities, devoid of the peaks of anger, and free from emptiness, one who possesses an even mind through practice should avoid the ways of the village. 10/10.
The past and the future, as well as the present;
the cognition of hearing from afar, and likewise the paralyzing of fetters, O Dear One. (10.11)
O Goddess, the seizing of animals, possession, the destruction of death, immortality, and likewise transformation—in brief, [these are the results]. (10.12)
Success comes through speech in this way; what does one do, O Beloved of the World?
The second [lotus] has eight petals and is brilliantly illuminated by the meditation on light.
Causing disturbances such as those in the city, death destroys [the practitioner] by means of traditional scripture;
it assumes many forms for one whose mind is solely intent on meditation. (10.14)
What must one do regarding the sovereign kings of the mandalas?
For when enraged, he can destroy the entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving. (10.15)
Constantly devoted to perpetual practice, he is the agent of creation and dissolution;
the third great wheel is the liberator from the nine principles.
Having meditated upon the desired object of desire for six months, that Guru shall [attain] the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, as well as the ability to see from a great distance.
O Goddess, he pierces even through hundreds of yojanas;
intent upon that meditation, assume many forms in solitude.
The fourth wheel, which is peaceful, increases happiness and joy;
indeed, one who is intent upon constant practice attains immortality. (10.19)
O beloved, by fasting for days, one brings about the end of life and the conquest of diseases;
indeed, through such fasting, one's life and death shall be overcome.
One may destroy [all defects] in a single day and night by means of this unsurpassed wheel;
through the yoga of constant practice, one shall attain the form of a sixteen-year-old. || 10/21 ||
O beautiful goddess, one should always contemplate the fifth [wheel] as a great eight-petaled lotus of smoky color; by doing so, O beloved, one may shake the three worlds. (10.22)
It effects the seizure of speech and brings about the supreme paralysis of an army;
the sixth wheel, however, for a king, has eight petals and a pericarp. (10.23)
It possesses the luster of molten gold, brings about the fulfillment of all desires, and encompasses both the past and the future, as well as the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
It bestows [these fruits], of this there is no doubt, when kindled by devotion and meditation;
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, the seventh [wheel] has the luster of the full moon.
O blessed lady, that mind directed toward Him bestows auspicious enjoyment and liberation, as well as the destruction of old age and death and the power of entering another body. (10.26)
O best of men among the members of the mandala, what should he do?
[He should prepare] the eighth [mandala], the Great Wheel, adorned with eight petals. (10.27)
O fair-eyed one, they certainly bestow virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation;
when meditated upon with passion, they always inevitably grant supreme yellow paralyzing power. (10.28)
O Goddess, study [of the mantra] with white [sindūra] on crystal bestows liberation;
with black [sindūra], killing is proclaimed; and with smoky-colored [sindūra], it always effects eradication.
This [mantra] is beneficial for the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya), white as a stream of cow's milk;
it should perform the agitation of the city, the paralysis, the trembling, the falling, and so forth. || 10.30 ||
And the eighth meditation is always that which has the brilliant luster of a blazing fire;
O Goddess, this meditation is established as eightfold for each [deity].
And Cāpa and Kañcukī, O Goddess, having prostrated themselves again and again, said:
"O Bhairava, today my birth among the Mahākauras has become fruitful. (10.32)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇītiyoginīkaula*, brought down by the venerable Śrīmacchaghnapāda and issued from Candradvīpa. || 10/10 ||
The eleventh chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, tell me the characteristic of the non-duality of the sacrificial pap (caruka)."
Being entirely free from all doubt, one who is fearless will certainly attain success. || 11.1 ||
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that which you have asked regarding this world so cruel and terrifying, I shall explain without doubt, as it crushes all fears. (11.2)
For one who is perpetually established in non-duality, perfection arises;
however, he who causes duality to exist is dragged away by the yogis.
O Goddess, he who has fallen from the samaya is a paśu; of this there is no doubt.
Having abandoned the state of duality, he should be permeated by the practice of non-duality. (11.4)
I shall proclaim the five nectars, the most secret of secrets;
it must be known as the Kula-observance, especially by those born of noble family. (11.5)
O Sulocanā, this was formerly practiced by practitioners desiring accomplishment, as well as by other lineage-teachers and those who have attained success within the Kula.
Having known this, O beloved of the Yoginīs, mental perfection (mānasī siddhi) shall arise;
if one desires the Kaula perfection, one should obtain the supreme five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then it is accomplished within the Yoginī; there shall be a gathering for the attainment of siddhi.
And then, O Goddess, they bestow the sacrificial pap (caruka) endowed with the five [nectars].
If it is given once by the Yoginīs, one becomes equal to them at that very moment;
or else, having understood this, the knower of the Kaula who is joined in yoga should consume it.
It is accomplished here without a doubt, freed from the web of obstacles; whatever is well-considered by the mind becomes common to the assembly of Yoginīs.
Faeces, urine, semen, blood, and marrow mixed together—these five are eternally pure according to the Kula tradition. (11/11)
O Goddess, the daily and occasional rites must be performed with great effort;
likewise, beef, cow-ghee, blood, cow-milk, and curd [are required]. (11.12)
One who is intensely eager for accomplishment should perform this rite on an auspicious occasion;
free from doubt and free from conceptual construction, one should perform this according to the Kula tradition.
Otherwise, O my beloved, liberation is not achieved at all.
Listen again to another qualification with a one-pointed mind. (11.14)
A dog, a cat, a camel, and a jackal, as well as a horse;
a tortoise, a crocodile, a boar, a kitten, and a crab. (11.15)
The śalākī, the kukkuṭa, and many various species of birds, as well as the śeraka, the deer, the buffalo, and the gaṇḍaka. || 11.16 ||
One should collect whatever other fish are available; such a beast gains the power and capacity of consciousness for seven future births. (11.17)
By whatever means possible, one should always consume the *ākṛṣṭi*;
O Dear One, one should worship the assembly of Yoginīs with edible foods, drinks, and so forth. (11.18)
One who desires long life should consume [the elixir] drop by drop;
one should prepare the three kinds of meat as sour, pungent, and sweet. (11.19)
For the purpose of satiating the deities, the appropriate liquor should be offered—
whether it is produced from trees, from roots, from flowers, or even from fruits.
O Dear One, one should offer *peṣṭī*, *mādhvī*, and likewise *gauṇḍī* during occasional rites (*naimittika*);
however, non-duality (*advaita*) must be practiced exactly as it has been described, and certainly not otherwise. (11.21)
When one who commits evil acts, relying on the conduct of non-duality, behaves otherwise,
they fall into the terrible hells of Avīci and Raurava.
"Let them speak to that beast who has abandoned non-duality;
he is proclaimed a beast in the Kula when standing in the midst of the assembly of Yoginīs. (11.23)
One should keep it secret, even more secret, guarding it with great effort, just as one would hide one's own son born from the womb of one's mother's paramour. (11.24)
One should always protect non-duality and practice that which is most secret in due order;
then the perfection of the powers of sovereignty, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, shall become mental.
He himself is the Guru, he himself is the Siddha, he himself is the disciple, and he himself is Śiva.
Ignorance is the bondage; knowledge is that which is to be known, and it is the liberation from what is to be known.
The partless one constantly perceives both pleasant and foul odors;
yet, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, he likewise remains unstained.
In the same way, O Goddess of the Gods, the yogi is not smeared by merit or sin;
[he regards] the sin of killing a Brahmin and so forth as equal to the fruit of the horse sacrifice and so forth. (11.28)
Even by bathing at all sacred fords or by contact with barbarians and the like, a yogi is clearly not affected by these acts, even when they are being performed. (11.29)

One should maintain equanimity, freedom from passion, and indifference toward the movements of the senses; being free from possessions, one should remain content and not allow oneself to be affected by the pairs of opposites. (11.30)
One should gradually abandon desire, anger, hypocrisy, and greed;
O auspicious lady, one should not criticize others, nor deviate from the non-duality of the sacred observance (samaya).
In that [place] where the physical body is produced, one should always drink the blood and semen;
this is the beloved *cāru* (delightful offering) for the *siddhas* and *yoginīs* at all times. (11.32)
Listen: meat is dear to the Śākinīs, and hear what is dear to the goddesses—vuka flowers, the water of Śiva, blood, semen, and likewise wine.
The spittle of a Brahmin and so forth, the fragrance of flowers and the like, incense, perfume, song, betel-leaf, and red garments—[these are not to be accepted]. (11.34)

O beloved, the first [deity] for protection is red in color; O auspicious one, the unfolding of higher knowledge for the perfected ones occurs in this way alone, not through the service of others. (11.35)
One should not have sexual intercourse with a woman of inferior birth, for she is fickle, always seeking her own pleasure, and a constant mocker of noble lineage and sacred scriptures. (11.36)

One becomes a vessel for accomplishment within six months by being impassioned through the sight of one's own power, by touch, by means of the characteristic marks, and through the enjoyment of the wisdom of the Kula.
One should always consume the water of Śiva and the *brahma* [liquor], even if it is devoid of the initial mantra; by doing so, one will attain union with the Yoginīs. || 11.38 ||
O Dear One, he should always perform the washing of the feet in that very manner, and he should also constantly wash the face of the Brahmins, O Beloved. (11.39)
One should never apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) made from the substances found in the womb or the testicles;
it destroys eighty types of wind-disorders (vāta) and cures the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha). || 11/40 ||
One is liberated from all diseases, just as a snake sheds its skin;
possessing a splendor like the rising sun, it is indeed eternally dear to the Yoginīs.
The three worlds come under one's control, as do the celestial dwellers beginning with Brahmā;
[one attains] the practice of non-duality regarding the sacrificial pap (caruka) and eating together with those born of mantra. (11.42)
O Goddess, one should perform everything under the influence of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);
one should not act by force without the will.
This practice of non-duality regarding the sacrificial pap (*caru*) is declared to be the definitive conclusion of knowledge.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Great Kaula, the *Jñānanirṇītiyoginī*, brought down by the venerable Śrī Śaghnapāda and issued from Candradvīpa. 11/11.
The twelfth chapter. The Goddess said:
O Goddess, with our hearts thrilled and satisfied, we are covered in a mantle of horripilation.
O Bhairava, I ask you again concerning that which has arisen regarding edible foods.
Today I [shall observe] the family commitment; today I [shall observe] that which is endowed with the characteristics.
Now I desire to hear the characteristics of the conduct of worthy vessels. (12.2)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Vīracāmuṇḍā, to the characteristics of the conduct regarding the vessels:
the first is in the form of a child, and the second has the appearance of a madman.
The third is in the form of a king, the fourth is Kaśmala, O beloved;
the fifth is Svātantrya, O Goddess, and the sixth is Vīranāyaka. (12.4)
O beloved, the seventh is named Gandharva, the eighth is Nagna, O Goddess; the ninth is Tridaṇḍa, and another is Vedavikraya. (12.5)
O beloved, whatever desire one forms, that very vow one should undertake;
having understood both the non-lineage (akula) and the lineage (kula), O beautiful lady, [one should know] the lineage of the Goddess.
Bhairava, who is endowed with supernatural powers, should be worshipped by those belonging to the [spiritual] families;
one whose mind is purified should worship one's own guru daily at the three times of day.
One should diligently offer service to one's own guru through thought, deed, and speech, with the desire to attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (12.8)
In the tradition of the Guru-Kaula, one who is imbued with devotion and the state of non-dual conduct should perform the desired vow in conjunction with non-duality.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, through your grace, the characteristics of the practice have been understood.
Once more, O Lord of Gods, I ask about the auspicious characteristics of worthy recipients."
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, listen with a one-pointed mind to the determination regarding the vessels:
those made of clay, those born of tortoise-shell, O Goddess, and those made of bell-metal, copper, or iron. (12.11)
O beloved, it may be made of gold or silver, or born of mother-of-pearl or conch;
O lady of excellent hips, it may also be of the *kaulika* type or otherwise made of glass.
O beloved, that which is produced from horn, from wood and the like, or originating from stone,
as well as the skull of Viśvāmitra— these are the best of all vessels, O beloved.
Having placed a small amount of that [substance] therein, one should drink it or eat some food; by doing so, both the husband and the wife shall become most excellent. || 12/14 ||
One should know that this large coconut shell is a vessel;
by the non-attainment of this vessel, one may drink liquor from another vessel. (12.15)
O Goddess, the characteristics of the vessels and the characteristics of the conduct have been told;
O Goddess, the true nature has been explained—what else do you ask now?
The Goddess said: "Today my divinity has become fruitful, O Sovereign of the Gods, O Leader of the Heavens;
by Your grace, O Lord of Gods, the definitive conclusion of knowledge is to be understood. (12.17)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the vessel of conduct (*caryāpātra-lakṣaṇa*), in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, brought down by the illustrious Śrīmacchaghnapāda from the great *Śrīyoginīkaula*. 12/12.
The Thirteenth Chapter. Bhairava said:
"O leader of heroes, listen to the realization that constitutes the conviction of liberation."
Having realized that food of liberation, the individual soul attains both the lower and the higher realms.
One should constantly utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa" regarding all that is moving and stationary within the body;
upon hearing this, his master attains the divine and auspicious supreme liberation.
Having known that which pervades the three worlds and in which the entire universe is established—that hidden true nature—omniscience arises. (13.3)
Without it, worldly transactions are not released; indeed, without it, there is no experience of the auspicious or the inauspicious anywhere. (13.4)
O Beloved, neither the mind nor the consciousness is to be grasped, nor is there anything to be drunk or retained;
for him whose mind has become transmental (unmanā), liberation occurs right here in this world.
When one beholds the garland of jewels flashing at the dvādaśānta, for that person there shall be liberation; he is no longer stained by sins or merits. (13.6)
For one whose mind is always devoted to the path of the gods and the Mahāyāna, there is no doubt that liberation will come, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. (13.7)
These two are in the testicles; these two are in the penis; these two are in the navel; these two are in the mouth.
*iv-au* in the right nostril; *il-au* in the left cavity; *ir-au* on the right.
The letter *i* is the right ear; the letters *ī* and *ś* are the left ear.
*Ihrai* at the center of the eyebrows; *saṃ taṃ* on the forehead; *saṃ aṃ* on the left ear.
He who is the right ear; he is the left eye.
He is the right eye.
That [breath] of yours is the left nostril; that [breath] is the right nostril for a male.
That is the face (rūṃ). That is the navel (yaṃ). That is the penis (ṣu/meḍhraḥ).
The syllable *laṃ* is in the anus.
O Goddess, for him in whose body this sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) proceeds, there is liberation preceded by supreme consciousness; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, when the skull is split open during the alms-gathering, then— || 13/8 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Nyāsa, in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, brought down by the venerable Śrīmacchendrapāda from Candradvīpa, according to the Great Śrīmat-Śaṃkara-Yoginī-Kaula tradition. 13/13.
The fourteenth chapter. The Goddess said:
[Tell me of that] which is free from the web of mantras and devoid of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
This supreme method, which brings about immediate accomplishment, is entirely free from the meditation on the wheel.
Listen, O Goddess, to this wonderful account concerning the exit within the body, which severs all doubt and produces great amazement. (14.2)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the gods suffer, being of dull intellect;
so too do the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Asuras, and those whose wealth is penance.
O Goddess, O Beloved, this supreme Kaula [teaching] has not been told to those who are devoid of devotion to the Kula and bereft of devotion to the Guru. (14.4)
The essential Kaula doctrine must not be given to disciples who have been poorly examined;
they are deceivers, misers, fools, and devoid of truth, O blameless one. (14.5)

One should not grant initiation to one who hates the gods, the sacred fire, or ascetics; however, if such a person should grant it to these disciples, the teacher's spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) is lost.
Always carrying out the commands of the guru, examining what is appropriate and inappropriate, always delighting in dharma, and being free from anger and emptiness. (14.7)
One whose mind is always serene through devotion to the gods, the sacred fire, ascetics, and yoginīs—being resolute, free from desire, guarded, and dwelling in solitude without doubt. (14.8)
One who is devoted to firm faith should choose a disciple and, having always examined him well, should grant him long life. (14.9)
These two types of persons are of a highly discursive nature and maintain hypocritical vows;
they are hostile toward the Yoginīs and transgress the commands of the Guru. (14.10)
The Kaula knowledge should not be given to one who is lustful, nor likewise to one who is wrathful; O Goddess, it should not be given to a defamer of Śiva, nor to a slanderer of Kulabhairava. (14.11)
In the collection of oceanic jewels, that which is priceless on earth is for sale;
for he possesses a hoard with which one could not purchase an ocean filled with gems.
O Goddess, a slanderer shall not [attain this] for seven days beyond;
O Great Goddess, this Kaula teaching is the definitive rule for all time. (14.13)

O beloved goddess, he who has no rivalry regarding the Kaula tradition and who desires to know such a supreme and perfect knowledge should cause [the disciple] to receive the seven... [initiations]. 14.14.
O Goddess, O noble lady, listen to that sequence which you have asked about:
first, O beloved, when one practices the root-cakra.
But then, O Goddess, that which produces great wonder becomes a sign:
first there is trembling, and the second is shaking. (14.16)
He was like a frog leaping about, performing various gestures such as shaking his hands, feet, and head, and speaking;
indeed, he was like one who has mastered the entire collection of mantras and mudrās.
O Goddess, [there is] the abandonment of the earth, poetic skill, as well as the past and the future, the deception of time, and the transformation of form.

O beautiful one, O lady of excellent countenance, this Mūlakaula indeed brings about the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, the power of moving through the sky, and the attainment of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis).
Listen, O Goddess, to this wonderful determination of the *ādhāra* itself:
above the wheel of the Goddess, O Queen of Gods, the *ādhāra* is four finger-breadths in extent.
And having fixed the mind upon that very [object], O Pārvatī, and having become pure, there arise trembling, paralysis, as well as speech, mudrās, and leaping. (14.21)

But those who have not heard the scriptures [will attain] the great multitude of mantras and mudrās, the path of the earth, the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), as well as subjugation and summoning. (14.22)
O Goddess, it removes old age and deceives the time of death; O beloved, mastery of the netherworld and the power of moving through the sky are attained before long.
Thus has the characteristic of the support been explained to you;
now I shall further declare the determination regarding the Brahma-knot.
O auspicious lady, having fixed the mind on that place for one watch of the night,
there will arise trembling, paralysis, and so forth, as well as various kinds of speech.
Hearing from afar, causing the agitation of cities, as well as knowledge of the past and future, the deception of time, O Goddess, and immortality—these are the fruits of poetic power. (14.26)
The mastery of powers such as *aṇimā* and the mental perfection (*mānasī siddhi*) shall arise;
this, O Goddess, has been told to you as the definitive resolution regarding the knot of Brahmā.
Hear from me now, O auspicious and illustrious lady,
the truth concerning that place of Tryambaka where the upward-growing hairs are located.
Having the appearance of blazing light and a radiance somewhat like lightning, one should meditate for seven nights, and a sign of attainment will arise. (14.29)
Trembling, paralysis, as well as speech, mudrās, and likewise leaping up;
entering a city, possession, subjugation, attraction, and so forth. (14.30)
The vision of the past and the future, as well as the distant; the destruction of wrinkles and gray hair, and the transformation of physical form. (14.31)
Through practice, one becomes devoted to the common [practice] of the Khecarīs.
This, O Goddess, has been told to you regarding the Kaulika [teachings] concerning the hair-pores and so forth.
O lady of virtuous vows, the Kaula tradition arising from Vṛṣaṇa has been told to you.
Listen, O giver of boons, eternal mother of heroes, to [the teaching] of the heroes. (14.33)
I shall now describe the practice of Vahnikaula;
having made the mind steady therein, one remains for even half a moment.

O Goddess, [this practice] effects gestures such as those of praise and speech, the relinquishing of the earth element and so forth, subjugation, attraction, and the destruction of old age and death. (14.35)
Entering the city, possessing it, and causing disturbances within the city—arise! The sword, the underworld, and the fixed [state] will certainly be accomplished for the Kaulika.
One who is constantly devoted to practice can assume whatever form one desires. Furthermore, I shall proclaim another supreme secret essence of the Kaula tradition.
Having fixed the mind within the heart, as long as it remains established therein,
for that long one attains samādhi, characterized by signs such as paralysis (stobha) and possession (āveśa).
The limbs, including the hands, feet, head, and so forth, tremble; there is also a bursting sensation of the skin or a shaking of the body, O bestower of boons. (14.39)
Whether she be a Gandharvī, a Kinnarī, or a Yakṣī dwelling in the netherworld;
whether she be an Asurī, O Mistress of the Gods, or a Vidyādharī with beautiful eyes. (14.40)
There is no doubt that one who is absorbed in that through practice becomes agitated; likewise, there is the knowledge of the past and the future, as well as hearing from afar. (14.41)
O one of great austerity, entry into the city, possession, the destruction of death, and union with the Yoginīs will clearly manifest before long. (14.42)
Thus has the true nature of your lineage, which resides within your heart, been revealed.
O Makaradhvaja, listen as I shall speak again of a further marvel.

Having focused the mind with effort on the source arising from the pit of the throat, O beloved, one should utter the true essence of the scriptures within the mouth, impelled by one's own power, O beloved. (14.44)
For him, there is no death in the past, the future, or likewise the present; for he is imperishable and possesses the splendor of the immortals.
O Goddess, it is free from old age and disease, devoid of wrinkles and grey hair; yet when enraged, it can shake the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu, nor the Rudras, nor even Rudra himself [is the cause]; rather, it is the nature of one's accomplishment and constant practice that determines the result. (14.47)
This Kaula tradition, which arises from the feet [of the Guru], does not consist of a self-determined ascertainment of knowledge;
this is the supreme knowledge, the knowledge of mental accomplishment in absolute freedom.
The true essence of knowledge, which is extremely secret and resides in the throat, has been declared;
it should be grasped with effort by one who desires accomplishment in the Kaula path. (14.49)
Thereafter, one should make the tongue upward toward the secret Lord who crushes all diseases, and fix the mind upon Him. (14.50)
O Dear One, one should practice that constantly; even for a moment, it destroys [suffering].
In an instant, one is liberated from diseases, as well as from illness, death, old age, and the like.
The multitude of diseases perishes, just as deer flee from a lion;
in an instant, the disease is destroyed, for this pungent [remedy] is a destroyer of leprosy. 14.52
O Great Goddess, by its sweet taste it destroys wrinkles and grey hair;
by the taste of milk, a man becomes wise and immortal. (14.53)

O Goddess, [the practice] is comparable to the taste of clarified butter; as for how independence may arise, one should direct the mind by means of the wheel and apply the *vijṛmbhikā* to the nose. (14.54)
Success indeed comes through speech alone; O beloved, one becomes like another Kāmadeva.
One may become a daughter of the gods, a celestial being, a Yakṣa, or a Vidyādhara. (14.55)
O beloved, having drawn in sweetmeats such as sugar-candies, *laṭṭukas*, *śokavartikas*, and many celestial maidens, they consume them.
O Goddess, [the powers] are *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and the upward flow of semen;
the yogi becomes one whose semen flows upward, O Beloved, and he who does not is not a yogi. (14.57)
One should not spit, even when speaking out of favor;
for this wheel is difficult to obtain, and there is no yoga higher than this.
Beyond this is the supreme secret, the most excellent Kaula of the Yoginīs;
when practiced through the repeated recitation of its words, it produces a great marvel.
The qualities beginning with *aṇimā* and likewise the vision from afar arise in him;
there is no doubt about this for those who are devoted to constant practice. (14.60)
O Goddess, [the powers of] raising the dead, entering another's body, causing an image to speak, and shattering jars and stones occur within that [state]. (14.61)
The seizing of animals, possession, and the transformation of form and so forth;
[the powers of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Yama, Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu as well. (14.62)
O fair-faced one, within the body are the Somarājas beginning with Svarga;
O beloved, there are Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas.
With a continuous succession of tens of millions of celestial palaces, adorned with every kind of ornament,
it was joined by the constellations and stars and struck against the shell of the universe.
One perceives the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, situated within the body; through constant meditation, one may manifest one's own physical form in manifold ways.
O Goddess, Śiva himself is the creator and destroyer by means of thousands of crores;
through practice, he bestows the eightfold supernatural powers (siddhis) enjoined by the scriptures.
O fair-faced one, it is honored by all the Siddhas as equal to myself;
this Kaula [teaching] should be given to the virtuous, and never to just anyone. (14.67)
In the tradition of the Guru-Kaula, one who is always devoted to the worship of the Goddess with devotion must remain firmly resolved that this extraction is to be kept perpetually secret.
Henceforth I shall speak; listen, O lady of noble lineage, having made one hundred thousand [recitations] while established in the mass of syllables on the forehead, O worshipper of the gods.
One speaks many kinds of words, and likewise there is the wandering of the limbs;
O Goddess, one emits a sound and a great agitation arises. (14.70)
O beloved, one who is intensely devoted to practice can assume whatever form they desire;
therefore, listen now to the supreme secret, both higher and lower.

O Hero, by constant practice, one should perceive that which resides in the mass of letters on the forehead in the center of the *brahmarandhra*, and one should abandon the ways of the village. (14.72)
O Dear One, he indeed becomes the agent of creation and destruction; there is no doubt. He is eternally liberated from old age and death, O Yoginī. (14.73)
O Goddess, by mere knowledge [of this], one attains liberation through practice;
hereafter, I shall declare the definitive determination of the skill regarding the apertures.
The wise one should practice constantly; for him, neither disease nor death exists.
Having become equal in power to me, he becomes the agent of both dissolution and creation. (14.75)
O auspicious one, he plays independently, assuming whatever form he desires; O Goddess, always remain steady in that consciousness, which is the emission of the Kaula.
O Goddess, they hear from afar; O Goddess, there is reflection and observation; O Beloved, the striking of the skull-bowl is established in secret.
O Goddess, by practicing this, one will always emerge from the outside, even if pursued by flies, gnats, tigers, lions, or elephants. (14.78)
O beloved, one should maintain this form mentally contemplated;
this is indeed the family-knowledge (kulavijñāna) transmitted through the succession of lineage. || 14.79 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, this very essence that bestows liberation must be known;
therefore, one should diligently understand all the characteristics of the Kula.
Like a jar filled with water, like walls and pillars, O Lord, the yogin remains pervading all, resembling a mountain. (14.81)
Henceforth I shall explain [the higher path]; listen, O Goddess honored by heroes!
One should not contemplate water, O Goddess, nor fire, wind, or space. (14.82)
Neither below, nor above, nor in the middle, O beloved, like a piece of wood or a clod of earth;
when the state of *unmanī* arises within the mind, O beautiful one, [then it is so]. (14.83)
Having made the mind empty of even emptiness, free from anxiety and established in immovability, the wise man perceives jars, cloths, pillars, villages, wells, and so forth. (14.84)

Even when being awakened by the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums, and by the resonance of lutes and flutes, the living soul does not wake up, having entered into a state of absorption in that [sound]. (14.85)
Past, present, and future, as well as the past and the future— having become indeed imperishable and immortal, he has Kāmadeva as his second.
O beautiful one, even while being split apart and bitten by serpents,
the Pārijāta tree remained as if a rain of flowers were falling upon it.
Hāṭakeśvara is worshipped by the daughters of the Nāgas according to their merit;
he consists of five streams and has been impelled by me for the sake of liberation.
O Goddess, impelled by devotion to you, this determination regarding the sphere of the Kula has been declared;
therefore, O Goddess, the defining characteristics of the determination of the mudrās are now being told.
