When the ring finger is joined at the heart, this is the seal that bestows lordship;
when one perceives a shimmering garland of jewels at the end of the twelve [fingers], [this is the sign]. (14.90)
This mudrā is called Anāmā; it bestows the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*).
O Dear One, it is sealed by the five mudrās and accompanied by consciousness.
One should split that door-panel, which is firmly secured by the bolt;
one should split it from the base up to the dvādaśānta by means of the movement of Śakti.

Having become a Yoginī through the Goddess and brought under the control of the circle of Mothers (mātṛcakra), they dissolve into the wheel of the Khecarīs; one should then agitate the supreme nectar.
O Goddess, O Beloved, how can there be immortality without nectar?
Listen: nectar is the true essence of the Kaula, consisting of the Kāmakalā.
O Dear One, the reality residing within the innate state is radiant and pure as a gem;
its likeness is like a pearl, yet it resembles a firefly.
Resembling the radiance of a star, it throbs in the expanse of the sky;
its forms are white, red, black, smoky, and yellow.
...the agent of creation and destruction, as well as both origination and dissolution, and that which is devoid of both Akula and Kula. || 14/97 ||
O Goddess, one should practice during the day, having fixed the gaze upon the sun;
then one's own true form is seen... || 14/98 ||
One should diligently practice the form of the other; of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, he effects creation and dissolution in an instant. (14.99)
O Goddess, at night one should practice [meditation on] the Lord, who possesses a hundred peaks and stands between two bows. || 14/100 ||
O Goddess, O auspicious one, that by which the moving and unmoving world was created is the supreme; into this very [source] everything goes to its dissolution, just as a river merges into the ocean.
By this mere firmness, one is not smeared by merits or sins;
O Dear One, the body consists of eight types and is the locus of the eight elements.
The consciousness of form is eightfold, and that which transcends form is likewise eightfold;
the wheel, as the cause of accomplishment, should be understood according to this rule of eight times eight.
O Dear One, she who arises from the *nalikā* and *vajra* is the family characteristic (*kulalakṣa*) and the support of the family (*kulādhāra*);
she is the agitation (*kṣobha*) and the vehicle of the family (*kulayāna*) for those who know the supreme reality.
O radiant one, it is authorized by the Gurus, Siddhas, and deities;
it is cool like the foam on milk-water and resembles the moon. (14.105)
In half a moment, he becomes agitated like the shore of the great ocean;
yet, during the great heat [of the practice], he is liberated from the multitude of diseases such as fever and leprosy.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on Meditation, Yoga, and Mudrās, in the *Jñānanirṇaya* of the *Śrīyoginīkaula*, brought down by the illustrious Śrīmac-Chaghnapāda and emerged from Candradvīpa. 14/14.
Fifteenth Chapter. The Goddess said:
Today my birth has become fruitful, and likewise my ascetic penance has borne fruit.
O Bhairava, by your grace, my status as a deity has today become fruitful.
Today my asceticism has borne fruit; today I am adorned with eyes.
Today I have achieved auspiciousness, having attained the patience of the vision of knowledge.
Today my ear has been adorned; I have heard the Great Kaula. Today the mass of splendor, the Great Knowledge, resides within my heart. (15.3)
Today my lineage and conduct have been purified; today my physical form and marks have been perfected;
today my delusion has been severed through your grace, O Lord of the Gods. (15.4)
Having realized that I did not previously ask at every step,
tell me everything regarding whatever possesses firm reality.
"Previously I had not studied this; yet you have pleased me again and again.
Among seven crores of Cāraṇas, it was asked of them: 'What is this? (15.6)
Formerly, when the world had perished in a terrible single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had been destroyed,
by what means, O Lord of Heroes, was your self protected? O Master, tell me that reality by which you protected yourself.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O possessor of great knowledge! This has never been asked by anyone.
It is extremely profound, O Goddess, and though it was well-guarded and hidden by me,"
O Bhairavī, behold it situated on the tips of the nails supported by the shaven heads;
everything is perfectly established within the center of the wheel of bones. (15.9)
This innate wheel, arising from the supreme name Vajra, through the application of vajra-yoga, a person becomes like a vajra. 15/10 ||
It has seven thousand million petals accompanied by filaments;
the auspicious wheel consists of half a million, one hundred thousand, and ten million [spokes].
Having wrapped it three times, one should place it in a vessel of milk;
then, with substances that extract the essence of milk, one should always fill that body.
In the pericarp is the supreme reality, resembling the flax flower;
it has five spokes, eight petals, and sixteen spokes, being most beautiful.
O fair-faced one, one should draw a sixteen-spoked [wheel] provided with intermediate spaces, and an eight-spoked lotus petal, as well as a single sixteen-spoked [wheel]. (15.14)
O you of excellent vows, a dot (bindu) must be placed as an interval;
indeed, the self, conjoined with the vital breath, is divided by sixteen syllables. || 15/15 ||
The division of sixteen syllables is established in the upper wheel;
furthermore, O Goddess, it consists of four parts and never otherwise. (15/16)
And having placed the self-wheel in the support (ādhāra) above that, one should cause it to be flooded by the upper wheel after having positioned the self within the pericarp (karṇikā). || 15/17 ||
O Goddess, being flooded by the overflowing streams of cow's milk,
he perceived himself as sixteen years of age, situated below.
O fair-eyed one, one should bathe the life-force wheel (*prāṇacakra*), which displays a certain radiant luster, with the previously mentioned wheel that is subtle and resembles the full moon. (15.19)
One should bring [the world] to a state of immobility by means of the arising of the wheel of bones;
having flooded the entire universe, one should practice the three wheels.
O Pārvatī, they have ascended to the summit of the lotus stalk, and even above that;
O beloved, how could they effect the withdrawal into the womb within the pericarp?
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, devoid of fever and disease, indeed imperishable, immortal, and eternal—remain thus, O Mānasa, as you deserve. (15.22)
When the withdrawal occurs, then one should behold the moving and the unmoving;
then, O auspicious one, O Mistress of Sound, he remains together with me.
Just as sovereignty over the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, belongs to me, so too, O Goddess, does he become the agent of creation and destruction. (15.24)
"O Sulocanā, with a mind always concentrated, let the skeletal frame remain firm like a vajra; O beloved, do not withdraw the body. (15.25)
"O beloved, this was practiced by me in the past; I am imperishable.
This has been declared by me in the scripture in immeasurable and manifold ways. (15.26)

This secret of mine, whose true nature is hidden and well-guarded, must be concealed with great effort; one should not transmit it beyond seven [generations]. This true nature of your lineage has been revealed to you by me.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Supreme Vajrīkaraṇa," brought down by the venerable Śrīmac-Chendrapāda from Candradvīpa, as contained within the *Yoginīkaula* concerning the determination of knowledge. 15/15.
The sixteenth chapter. The Goddess said:
O Bhairava, [you who are] endowed with yoginīs and siddhas, and possessed of a divine form!
Standing in the midst of his Mothers, he sports with his own power out of pride in his strength.
O Protector, your conduct and activities are always difficult to comprehend;
they were not understood even by the gods and gandharvas, much less by those born upon this earth. (16.2)

You abide in the field (kṣetra) three times a day, or perhaps in the field on the mountain-pīṭha. Tell me that, O Lord of Gods; O God, tell me of the divine vision of the foods for one who knows supreme meditation, O Lord. (16.3)
Bhairava said:
"Well asked, O blessed lady, whose domain is the wondrous siddhis! As it is being told, O large-eyed one, what fear do you have, O passionate woman? (16.4)
Śrīśaila, Mahendra, and the renowned seat called Māyāpīṭha— O auspicious lady, I am indeed present there at the assembly for the attainment of the three times.
O auspicious Mistress of the Family, those men who are serene and whose minds are one-pointedly absorbed in the meditation on the void shall have a vision of me there together with you.

On Śrīśaila, perfection is attained; on Mahendra, it is remembered as being characterized by passion (rājasa); Kāmākhya is remembered as the seat (pīṭha) associated with the virtuous and joined with yoga.

Having obtained a gathering (melāpaka) at that place, one attains the siddhis of the Yoginīs; likewise, whatever form is conceived by the mind, such as the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), [is attained]. (16.8)
But you have learned of my conduct and behavior; you have told me of the place of meeting, and you have heard of my auspicious deeds. (16.9)
And that which consists of the five streams, hidden and within the sphere of accomplishment, is enjoined as food by the Lord; otherwise, it is never [to be consumed].
I am that supreme reality; I am Bhairava, O beloved;
I am Sadāśiva, Īśa, Śrīkaṇṭha, and indeed Rudra as well. (16.11)
I am that fisherman, O Goddess; I am Vīreśvara, my dear.
"I am Ananta, O Great Goddess; I am Rudra, O beautiful lady of the gods.
I dissolve the entire universe; I am the dissolution, O Mistress of the Kula. (16.13)
Furthermore, O Goddess praised by the wise, I am the moving and the unmoving, the creation, and the creator;
as the Ordainer in the Kula tradition, I eternally protect that which has been established. (16.14)
That by which it is sung as "Viśvapāda" because it is pervaded by Viśva, and that which is renowned as "Vicitrā" because of its manifold and variegated creation; || 16.15 ||
I sport according to my own will, and I create and transform;
O Goddess, I am Śvetapāda, and thus I am celebrated as Śvetapāda.
Your splendor is like the moonstone, the color of a bumblebee, and perfectly pure;
we two, O bestower of boons, are renowned in the world as Bhṛṅgapādās.
"O beloved, I am the lord of both the Asuras and the Suras;
O beautiful one, my name is renowned as Bhaṭṭapāda."
Those who long for prosperity (śrī) are called Śrīkaṇṭha by him.
O Great Goddess, I am Rudra, whose form is fierce (rūru), O you who delight in the destruction of [evil]. (16.19)
"O Great Goddess, O beloved, you who have beautiful limbs and who cause the mountains to tremble;
O Great Goddess Umā, I am your husband, my dear. (16.20)
O Lord of Śrī, O Śrīnātha, in the domain of the Siddhas,
when knowledge was brought down by you and me in the form of Kāma,
then that very reality was brought down for you and for Ṣaṇmukha.
Therefore, O Goddess, beloved of the Praṇava, in the Kaula tradition,
I exist in the form of the Unmanifest on the Island of the Moon, O Beloved.
Therefore, O beloved, that which belongs to my family is the unmanifested sphere of experience.
The Goddess said:
"For what purpose, O Lord, did I go to Candradvīpa? And for what reason were the wise ones swallowed by the primordial Ṣaṇmukha? (16.23)
O Goddess, there is yet another wonder for one who desires success in Kaulava:
that which was indicated for the sake of indication is known by the name Vaṭuka.
O Bhairava, I wish to hear about the castes and about meditation alone.
Bhairava said: O beloved speaker, although you perceive yourself as the Lord,
you are indeed Desire, the Power of Knowledge, and the one called the Power of Action, O radiant one.
Gaurī, Mahākālī, and Lakṣmī with that very Śrī—O large-eyed one, I and you are the ones who cause all the scriptures to descend [into the world]. (16.26)
And when I went with you to the Moon Island,
Kārttikeya arrived there in the form of a young boy.
Resorting to a state of ignorance, the scripture was then indeed stolen;
O Goddess, I myself instructed Ṣaṇmukha regarding the deceptive mouse and the rice-grains.
"O blessed lady, I went to the ocean to observe it with the vision of knowledge;
having drawn out a fish, O beloved, its belly was split open. (16.29)
Having taken it from within the belly of the fish and brought it back, the householder then established it;
my secret *jñānapaṭṭa* was thus preserved. (16.30)
Again, O Goddess of the Suras, being enraged by this very mouse,
he was cast into a pit and then thrown back into the ocean by means of a tunnel.
Having consumed ten billion portions of human flesh,
my wrath arose and I unleashed a web of spears.
A great fish, equal in strength to me, was drawn from the lake of the ocean by the seven sages; yet he has not come to me, O beloved. (16.33)
Born from the splendor of primordial wisdom, he was invincible even to the gods;
for at that time, the state of Brahmā—which consists of the mind and the nature of the fisherman—was indeed abandoned.
"I am that fisherman, O Goddess; I took up the profession of a fisher. Having then hauled out a fish, I was made equal to the wielder of the spear. (16.35)

Having burst open that "fish-belly" (matsyodara), it was taken up according to the Kula tradition; those who know this are said in the world to be liberated, while those devoid of such knowledge are called bound souls (paśus).
The Goddess said:
"O one of great merit, you are a Brahmin; I have made you a fisherman.
O Brahmins, those who kill fish are well known as 'matsyaghna' (fish-killers)."
Since he performed the work of a fisherman, the leader of the brahmins became a fisherman.
Bhairava said:
O Great-Souled One, O Beautiful One, it was formerly established by the Unmanifest;
therefore, O Most Compassionate One, that which is within the sphere of the Unmanifest has been born through the Kulas.
And for you, O Great Goddess, and for the Six-faced One, O Pārvatī;
and for Vighneśa, Nandin, and the wise Mahākāla—(39) [of these, I am the lord].
O Dear One, Jayā, Vijayā, and the others—Harasiddhi and Mahābalā—are renowned as Kālikā Yoginīs; they are situated above me, equal to me. (16.40)
O auspicious lady, this is indeed Akula where I abide;
at the end of the kalpa and at the end of the yuga, it remains within my body.
O Goddess, when [the soul] is within the living being, it is endowed with flowers, roots, and fruits, as well as leaves and branches, just like the growth of a tree. (16.42)
In the same way, O lady of noble family, even those others produced within my body,
O Goddess, O leader of the gods, have become bound souls (paśu) due to their state of ignorance.
But having received it again, O Goddess, that which is proclaimed as the Great Knowledge was told to you, O seeker of desire, and to the six-faced Gaṇa. (16.44)

Nandī is in Mahākāla; Jayā and Vijayā are in [the temples] beginning with Vijaya; Bhaṭṭā and others are in the temples beginning with Droṇaka; and likewise Harasiddhikā is [in the temple] beginning with Hara.
The yoginī Kālikā has declared the definitive teaching of the entire Kaula tradition;
let all who possess devotion and equanimity listen to this Kaulika doctrine. 16.46
From the Mahākaula comes the Siddhakaula, and from the Siddhakaula [comes] the Masādara;
I have proclaimed this descent according to the division of the four ages.
In the first [age], there is the determination of knowledge; in the second, that which is known as the Great Kaula;
in the third, it is named Siddhāmṛta; and in the Kali age, O beloved, it is Matsyodara.
And those who have emerged from this, O Goddess, I shall describe to you in their entirety;
from this *Yoginīkaula*, in the determination of knowledge. (16.49)
In an instant, the Yoginī was delighted; together with the Goddess and Vināyaka, the four Kulasiddhas, being well-cultivated, began to inquire.
With their hair standing on end like a cloak and holding flowers in their hands, they were all awakened;
prostrating themselves like a staff, they all said, "O Lord, speak the doctrine of the Self!"
But for those devoted to the practice of yoga, there is the definitive teaching on the protection of the vital essence (rakta-pāla).
Bhairava said:
"O large-eyed one, you and I have come together at Candradvīpa;
we have become the six-faced Vaṭuka in the lineage of the Kṣetrapālas. (16.52)
Seven crores have been perfected; for that long you were the protector of the field.
O fair-faced one, why are the two Vaṭukas not recognized as your sons, who are equal to you?
In the *Siddhāmṛta*, however, it is stated that the censure of the guru is condemned;
[the result] born from such truthfulness fell into the great ocean, having been cast down by Acyuta. (16.54)
In the most terrible Kali age, even though he was accomplished through divine means,
he incurred the very curse that has been proclaimed in every tantra.
I shall describe in brief his worship, the bali offering, the ritual cake (piṇḍa), the seat, and the recitation itself, so that it may be accomplished by the practitioner.

*Hrīṃ! To Vaṭuka, with tawny matted hair and tawny eyes, son of the Goddess, son of the Mothers—accept, accept this *bali* offered by me! *Curu murū hrīṃ!* O *balimantra*, move, move! Devour! (200 times).
This is the *piṇḍamantra*. Whatever the wise man may eat, he should first offer that as a *piṇḍa*.
*Hrīṃ* is the seat-mantra for Vaṭuka. *Hyauṃ hyauhyaṃ*, O Mahābhairava, is the mantra for worship.
*Hrīṃ hrāṃ* is the mantra for recitation.
He who always performs this recitation shall be free from obstacles and become a recipient of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One should say, "Take it, take it! and the Vaṭuka likewise takes it.
One should always meditate upon Vaṭuka, the crusher of obstacles, who holds a staff in his hand, wears matted hair, possesses the splendor of Brahman, and is clothed in red garments. (16.58)
Always being worshipped, with Daṇḍapāṇi at his front, he conquers the fourfold army and acts as a pillar for the camels. (16.59)

Against thieves, royal families, and the like, or against snakes, tigers, elephants, and so forth, one should perform the recitation of this mantra: "Hrīṃ Ca Vaṭuka Hrīṃ. This increases one's freedom from fear. (16.60)
It shall destroy all the wicked, just as elephants [are destroyed] by a lion;
wherever there are various minor accomplishments (kṣudrasiddhi) enjoined by the scriptures, [this destroys them]. // 16.61 //
O beautiful goddess, one should perform [the rite] with the mantra of Vaṭuka beginning with *hrīṃ*;
thus, one who desires success in the Kaula tradition should diligently worship Vaṭuka, who is honored by the Siddhas, with the syllable *hrīṃ* as the root of the mantra. (16.62)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, within the *Mahāyoginīkula*, in the descent of the venerable Matsyendra, originating from Candradvīpa. 16/16.
The seventeenth chapter. The Goddess said:
O Lord, regarding that determination of the discourse on the Self which was requested by me—
Now I wish to hear; speak without doubt, O Lord.
Bhairava said:
Well done, O Goddess, great Yoginī, leader of the Siddhas and Yoginīs!
[You have asked about] that which is secret, hidden, and closely related to the heart-lotus, which is turned downwards. (17.2)
The wheel that paralyzes the vital breath (samīrastobhaka) is cool at the knot of the uvula;
it is situated between the eyebrows, extending from the tip of the nose to the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta). || 17.3 ||
The forehead and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), situated at the peak and possessing great splendor—this elevenfold consciousness is said to be within the center of the body. (17.4)
Human beings suffer excessively because they do not know the traditional lineage (kulāgama);
that innate deity residing within the heart is said to be worthy of remembrance. (17.5)
The letter *ha* is eternally partless (*niṣkala*), while the letter *sa* is likewise with parts (*sakala*).
The letter *sṛ*, however, is always creation; thus, one should dissolve the universe with the syllable *hi*.

They say that the letter *sa* is the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and the letter *ha* is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); they call *ha* the vision (*īkṣa*), which is the supreme, great goal attained.
There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti;
they function in mutual dependence, O beloved, just like fire and smoke. (17.8)
There is no shadow without a tree, nor a tree without a shadow;
likewise, a yogi devoted to the practice of power attains equality within the Kula.
O Dear One, having known the gross, the subtle, and the supreme— the two swans who are the self of all—
one should understand the supreme Kaula doctrine, which has come down through oral tradition from ear to ear.
It should not be given to one who has not been examined; it should be given only to one who has been thoroughly examined.
Having performed the family initiation, one's own realization should be made manifest. (17.11)
O Goddess of gods, the five jewels and so forth are to be known from the Kula scripture:
the first is the arresting of grey hair, and the second shall be the attainment of one's desires. (17.12)
The third is the power of assuming any form at will; the fourth is the portion of the imperishable;
and the fifth is the great jewel that destroys old age and death. || 17.13 ||
Having assumed the divine preta-posture, unsupported at the *dvādaśānta*, in a solitary place within an underground chamber well-perfumed with fragrant incense; 17.14.
Having put on white garments, one should mark with sandalwood paste and place a couch there, provided with a good companion.
In the great sleep of universal pervasion, one neither hears nor sees;
whether it be a sweet fragrance or a foul stench, such as that of camphor, sandalwood, and the like. (17.16)
The knower of reality does not perceive smell; this, O Dear One, is the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti).
In that state, there is the deception of time—of both the past and the future.
O Goddess, O Mother of Heroes, he who has been described becomes both the creator and the destroyer;
the Haṃsa sports above and below, and again dissolves at the end of the twelve.
Situated in the heart, it becomes motionless like water within a jar;
resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk, it is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
Devoid of both the container and the contained, it is omniscient and manifest in every direction;
it moves by itself upward and downward, and again by itself.

One delights in the innate reality (sahaja-tattva) as it is within oneself, so too within others; having known this reality, O Goddess, O Beloved, those bound by the fetters of worldly existence [are liberated]. (17.21)
Placing the ear at the heart, the characteristic of the *haṃsa* is to be known;
in the region of the throat, the divine sound is entirely both *parā* and *aparā*.
From the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, that which is called Vāmā is coiled in shape;
it rises from its station in the anus and dissolves again at the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
Thus does the Haṃsa move within the body amidst the auspicious and inauspicious;
it is unstained, partless, upward-tending, pure, and utterly stainless.

O Lord, the Nigarbha, which is profound and characterized solely by eternal bliss, is the supreme state attained through great knowledge; it must be known as existing in the form of the embryo (garbha). 17.25
It is known as immeasurable, inconceivable, and the state beyond practice;
it is joined with inhalation and exhalation, and endowed with both existence and non-existence. (17.26)
He wanders among beings within the fourfold collection of living creatures;
he is the self, he is the agent himself, and he indeed withdraws the physical body. (17.27)
For the individual aggregate (piṇḍa) there would thus be suffering, while for the bound soul (bandha) alone there is supreme happiness;
it takes away dejection as well as old age and death.
Hunger, thirst, delusion, fear and the like, as well as greed, poverty, bondage, and so forth—O fair-eyed one, these belong to the physical body alone. (17.29)
And it is not cut by weapons, nor by a powerful wheel;
it is not pierced even by the thunderbolt, nor is it consumed in fire.
Death shall not come through water, nor shall life exist in water;
there shall never be delusion, nor passion, nor pride, nor envy. (17.31)
Neither greed, nor anger, nor anxiety afflicts him, O bestower of boons upon all beings; for all this [affliction] belongs to the senses. (17.32)
The world was created by the Jīva; that Jīva is the leader of the principles (tattvas).
That Jīva is the Pudgala, the Haṃsa, that Śiva, the all-pervading Supreme. (17.33)
O blessed lady, that is called the mind, which pervades all that is moving and unmoving;
having known the self by means of the self, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (17.34)
The Guru is indeed the primary Self; he may bind the Self again.
But the Self, as the master of itself, can also liberate the Self from bondage. (17.35)
Having known the self by means of the self—that the self indeed possesses the form of the body—and having known that which is other than the self, O Goddess, he is the king of yogis. (17.36)
He is called Śiva directly; he is liberated and is the supreme liberator.
O Goddess, he is eternally perfectly pure, like a lotus situated in the mud.
Relying upon this human body as a mere lump of flesh, that Śiva sports upon the earth;
O beautiful lady, by whomsoever such a Supreme Self has been known. (17.78)
By the mere touch of him, liberation occurs; of this there is no doubt.
And by obtaining his leavings, O beloved, supreme liberation shall be attained.
O Goddess, when one has been bathed by that very person with oil-massage and dry rubbing, and touched by that foot, he too becomes a recipient of liberation. (17.40)
By eating even a single morsel of that [food], one has indeed eaten the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Whatever merit a man obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), knowing this, he should apply his mind to it and obtain a fruit even greater than that. (17.41)
One should proclaim the true nature of the Yoginīs and Siddhas among the hosts of Vīras and Mothers; above this, indeed, is that auspicious state which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, brought down by the venerable feet of Indrācārya from the *Mahāyoginīkula* and originating from Candradvīpa. 17/17.
The eighteenth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the worship of the Siddhas consists of the realization that they reside within one's own body."
O Lord, please describe briefly the arrangement of the islands of the family.
For one desiring success, what would the consecration (abhiṣeka) during the Kaulava lunar day be like? || 18.1 ||
Bhairava said:
Well spoken! I shall describe the ritual for the island of the Kula, [using] either barley and other grains, rice flour, or flour derived from wheat. (18.2)
O Surasundarī, having consecrated any kind of flour with the *hrīṃ* mantra, one should fashion it into twelve wicks. (18.3)
One should worship the perfected Yoginī and the Guru at the side [of the vessel], which is beautifully adorned with milk, sugar-candy, and other delicacies, and filled with ghee. (18.4)
One should worship the Krama once, twice, or thrice a day;
one should always worship it first, for the Foremost Leader is the first of all that is consumed. (18.5)
One should recite the supreme and most excellent seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, which is dear to the Yoginīs;
for in this [mantra] lies the assembly of Yoginīs, which always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now I shall further explain the consecration within the sphere of the family:
one should fill the red [vessel] with blood, equal to that of the semen, O Beloved. (18.7)
With the very substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, honey combined with ghee, the red *vāmāmṛta*, semen, liquor mixed with *brahma*, [one should worship]. (18.8)
Combined with *vuka* flowers and mixed with black liquor (*kṛṣṇāsava*), the consciousness of joy from wine belongs to the Great Self when joined with devotion. (18.9)
One should extract the *druma* mantra, as well as the *guru*, the *siddhas*, and the deity:
*hrīṃ klīṃ mhau juṃ saḥ*.
Having worshipped [the deity] residing in the conch or the water-pot (*kalaśa*) according to the sequence, || 18/10 ||
For one who possesses firm devotion to the Lord of Gods, the preceptor is one whose aim is steadfast;
all the medicinal herbs beginning with Jayā and ending with Mohanā [are present], with palms joined in reverence. (18.11)
Endowed with the five jewels and encircled by a red thread, [one should offer] salt, milk, curd, clarified butter, wine, water, and sugarcane. (18.12)
One should describe in sequence the Svādudañca and Garbhāda,
as well as those eight Kulaparvatas, one by one in the mouth and in the center.
Or else, the preceptor, having likewise lifted [the substance] with his own hands from the courtesans or young maidens, should place it upon the head; then he will become a yogin. (18.14)
Furthermore, I shall describe the sacrifice; listen to me as I explain it correctly.
Taking a red cloth, or one that is variegated and auspicious, || 18.15 ||
Then, O Goddess, being well-composed, one should joyfully worship the Krama with unbroken grains of śāli rice, or with other divine and very beautiful offerings. (18.16)
Adorned with various ornaments, one should worship that auspicious sequence with sixty-four-fold rites using divine, fragrant flowers. (18.17)
The teacher, having become well-disposed and having gathered all the necessary requisites, becomes as beloved as a mother to the yoginīs, siddhas, and vīras. (18.18)
O beloved, it should be provided with wine and meat, along with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten;
it should be filled with ghee, sugar-candy, and sugar.
One should give jars and other excellent gifts, by the thousands or even by the hundreds; or sixty-four, or eight, or even seven. (18.20)
Having offered honor to the Guru, one should perform especially the worship of the Guru;
then, having performed the worship of the Vīra, by which he may be pleased again and again. (18.21)
The wise one should consume the *caruka*; he must not give it to one who lacks the pledges (*samaya*).
Especially by way of transmission from mouth to mouth, he becomes a partaker of accomplishment; otherwise, he is common. (18.22)

The general procedure has been described; [now] the specific method for the jar and the conch-face is taught according to the sequence stated in the scriptures. Having performed the worship while equipped with all necessary materials, one then becomes fit for accomplishment by merely undertaking this. || 18.23 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, belonging to the *Mahākaula* that emerged from Candradvīpa. 18/18.
The nineteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me now of the lotus situated within the body of the Siddhas.
Bhairava said:
All of them, possessing divine forms and great splendor, entered the wheel of the Goddess.
One who desires liberation should always meditate upon the beloved Self in the midst of all sixteen forms—auspicious and clad in white garments. (19.2)
One should always contemplate [the goddesses] as desiring youth; one should meditate on them as being dark-complexioned, wearing red garments, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents. (19.3)
The Siddhayoginī is adorned with red garments and red garlands;
in the midst of that, O Goddess, one should meditate upon oneself in that very form. (19.4)
One should always meditate with the mind upon Śrīnātha together with the Yoginīs in the form of a multitude, radiant and holding a conch in hand; thus one shall obtain whatever is contemplated.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya* of the *Mahāyoginīkula*, as brought down by the venerable Mīnapāda. 19/19.
The twentieth chapter. Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this wonder in this world which provides the conviction of liberation.
O Lord, O Beloved, one should press the throat, heart, and other areas while holding the breath upwards.
O beautiful one, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should cast the upward-moving vital force (utpāta) upwards;
then the skull is shattered and the life-force (jīva) goes to the stainless state (nirañjana).
O fair-faced one, that Śiva, having become all-pervasive, is the creator and the destroyer;
he knows himself as the Supreme and likewise knows the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
For him there shall be no suffering, and for him there shall be uninterrupted happiness.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should now always practice the other [method] which is directly perceptible.
Constantly devoted to the practice of his capacity, with food and sexual intercourse strictly controlled, he should press upward with the ring finger the navel and likewise the heart. (20.5)
Having made the mind, which has reached the dark thread and is situated at the tip of the power (śakti),
equal to one's own vital breath, it should be established at the foremost point of the movement of that power.
O beloved goddess, if one wavers due to practice [of other objects] such as flowers or images,
one should practice for six months with the breaths turned away from the upward direction.
One may travel from country to country for many years within the Lord of Gods;
the practice of entering another's body has thus been described to you.
Now, O auspicious Vīranāyikā, listen to another [account] concerning the hero Kulāśakti; likewise, hear the other characteristics of his Śakti. (20.9)
O auspicious lady, that power which is without beginning or end, known as Will (iccha) and born from Śiva, is Vyomamālinī; she is called Khecarī.
She who is called Vāmā is named Kuṇḍalinī, and Jyeṣṭhā is indeed Manonmanī;
she is renowned as Rudraśakti and is sung of as Kāmākhyā.
It is the foremost of all, being written but not recited;
it is celebrated in all scriptures as the *mātṛkā* and the multitude of sounds (*śabdarāśi*). (20.12)
The Goddess said: "The power of knowledge has been understood by me; O Lord, speak now of the powers of action.
Bhairava said:
I shall describe, in brief, the characteristics of a hero's power.
She has excellent white eyes, hair with curled tips, teeth like moonlight, a beautiful form, and speaks charmingly. (20.14)
She is endowed with devotion to her family, a worshiper of the Guru and the Goddess, beautiful in form, of pleasant disposition, with lovely eyebrows and a beautiful forehead. (20.15)
Through the family tradition, her devotion is free from fear;
the auspicious Goddess is of excellent character, fortunate, and a bringer of joy to people. 20/16
The wick of knowledge is protected as something rare in the midst of the world;
hear now the characteristics of the hero whose power is of such a nature. (20.17)
Handsome, of excellent character, truthful, and resolute; devoted to the Kula tradition of the Guru, firm in resolve, and free from anger. (20.18)
A great hero, ever fortunate, and endowed with confidence in his own body—
such a heroine you shall become, for you are presided over by the power of Rudra.
That fire is the Great Liṅga, the cause of creation and sustenance;
having realized it as the form of the Bindu, one becomes intent upon the rows of shimmering flames.
Akṣobhya, who is the source of all powers and is inwardly illumined by his own power,
having thoroughly understood the power born of the body, then [proceeds] to the grasping of that power.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, and cultivated in the practice of non-duality—such is devotion in the Kulakaula Āgama; such are the characteristics of a hero.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya* of the *Yoginīkula*, brought down by the venerable Mīnapāda and originating from Candradvīpa. || 20/20 ||
The Twenty-first Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, tell me the summary of the conduct within the sphere of the Kula."
Bhairava said:
I shall explain, without doubt, the characteristics of the conduct of the compendium (saṃgrahācāra).
O Goddess, the fifty-five-fold system is indeed the characteristic of Yoga;
its determination according to its divisions and subdivisions is found in the Kaula scriptures. (21.2)
The Kulapañcāśikāmūla, as well as the Kulasāgara, the Kulaugha, the Hṛdaya, and likewise the Bhairavodyānaka. || 21.3 ||
Candrakaula, Veṣṭi, and likewise Jñānanirṇaya—within these, that which is renowned by the name Sambara has emerged. (21.4)
Sṛṣṭikaula, Mahākaula, and likewise another, Timira; Siddhāmṛta-kaula and likewise another, Mātākaula. (21.5)
O Goddess of the gods, there is the Śaktibheda, the Kaula, and the unsurpassed Ūrmikaula; throughout the four ages, there is the conjunction of the Jñānakaula.
Likewise, there is Siddheśvara and another, the Kaula born of the Vajra;
and the Meghaja, which has emerged from that Kaula at a distance. || 21/7 ||
O Goddess, the nectar that flows forth from the touch of the limbs likewise issues from the Vajradāka;
[this occurs] on the full moon, the new moon, the eighth, and the fourteenth day.
One should offer as an oblation a live fish, liquor, and meat;
furthermore, the exposition must be performed by a preceptor who is free from doubt. (21.9)
Neither the lunar day nor the asterism, nor fasting, is prescribed;
wherever the yogi may be situated, he should thus take refuge in knowledge alone.
This true essence of the Kaula has been declared in the determination of knowledge. (21.10)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, within the *Mahāyoginīkula*, brought down by the venerable Mīnapāda and originating from Candradvīpa. 21/21.
The Twenty-second Chapter. The Goddess said:
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence... O Beloved, today I am yours.
Today, O Hara, I have accomplished my purpose through Siddhivināyaka.
And Ṣaḍmukha, Mahākāla, the Yoginī Kālikā, Nandīśa, Bhaṭṭakā, and likewise Droṇakā... || 22/2 ||
The highly fortunate Vijayā, the six Yoginīs, and the Mothers—O Bhairava, even I am not satiated with the Kaula nectar, nor are any of them. (22.3)
Bhairava said:
O blessed lady, that which was previously concealed has now been made manifest;
it should be declared in the Kula tradition for the deities in the world of mortals.
And the lineage (kula) of the Siddhas must be especially proclaimed,
as well as the non-dualistic knowledge of those who abide in duality, which is endowed with the conduct of the samaya.
Always concealing his sectarian marks, he was ever intent on the worship of the Guru;
he was affectionate toward all people and endowed with compassion for all living beings.
Having heard the words of Bhairava, their every hair standing on end like a coat of mail, they all, with satisfied minds, prostrated themselves upon the ground like staffs.
All the lords of the gods were devoted to their noble nature and had accomplished all that was to be done.
Today my dense thicket, obscured by the veil of ignorance, has perished; today the vast tree of saṃsāra has been cut down by you, O Lord. (22.8)
Today, the net of snares and the torrent of darkness have been severed, and the doubt regarding suffering has ended;
likewise, fifty million [verses] are the definitive conclusion of knowledge by name.
O Lord, in its midst, this essence has been extracted;
this scripture exists in every house of the yoginīs in Kāmarūpa.
O Goddess, by the grace of this knowledge, they constantly perform acts of restraint and favor, as well as the accomplishment of melāpaka.
O Sulocanā, the great scripture Candradvīpa has descended;
it is sung of as the state within the belly of the Great Fish, O Mistress Kāmākhyā.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, within the *Mahāyoginīkula*, brought down by the venerable feet of Matsyendra and originating from Candradvīpa. || 22/22 ||
The Twenty-third Chapter. The Goddess said:
O God, how do the Yoginīs move about upon the earth during the Kaulava [karana]?
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods; those on the surface of the earth know it through devotion.
Bhairava said:
O beautiful lady, hear now of the movement of the deities within this mortal world:
Kapotikā, Gṛdhrī, Haṃsī, and likewise Nakhī. (23.2)
The lame one... the speaker, O beautiful one, is the Kokābhāṣī; likewise the owl, the peacock, the Sararī, and the Gūlī. (23.3)
A female jackal, a goat, a buffalo (or camel), a female cat, a mongoose, as well as a tigress, an elephant, a peahen, and a hen... [are not... 23/4.
Whatever other forms are established upon the surface of the earth,
the Yoginīs take on those forms and sport upon the ground.

O auspicious lady, when [the planets] fall upon families or lords of families that consume what is unfit for consumption, their specific forms are described; one should understand them with focused attention. 23/6.
O Dear One, [the deities are] Haya, Nakhara, Sarpa, Citrika, Utmānasa, Vṛścika, Adhyantara, Āna, Mūṣaka, and Dardura. (23.7)
Through the nature of planets and spirits, with the perils of flaming fire and weapons, [they afflict] the Vedas... and likewise the kings of diseases and thieves. (23.8)
Likewise, Vidyuttuṅga, Gaṇḍa, Vyāghra, Siṃha, and Gaja—through these various forms and appearances, they produce manifold kinds of fear. (23.9)
And the sixty-four yoginīs protect the practitioner;
having assumed such forms, they quickly seize that victim. (23.10)
One must never show anger toward the Lord of the Gods while he is speaking, nor ever toward young maidens or women while they are speaking. (23.11)
At all times and according to one's ability, women who have undertaken a vow must be honored with diligence, as must young maidens by those belonging to noble families. (23.12)
With *punnāgas*, *nāgacaṃpas*, and others, with *mucukundas* and *pāṭalas*, with divine *pārijātas* and with *dāḍimas* radiant with blossoms; (13)
With *bandhūka* trees blooming with flowers, *campaka* trees radiant with blossoms, and with *jāti*, *utpala*, *kadamba*, *karṇikāra*, and *siṃhakesara* trees; (14) [23.14]
One should meditate upon her wearing red garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents, and adorned with lotuses, auspicious flowers, and śāla blossoms. (23.15)

One should constantly meditate upon oneself as the heroic Yoginī, adorned with a garland of jewels; one should avoid external worship. O auspicious lady, this worship has been described as the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, within the *Mahāyoginīkula*, brought down by the venerable feet of Matsyendra and emerged from Candradvīpa. 23/23.
The twenty-fourth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord Bhairava, today your compassion toward me has become fruitful."
O Lord, sovereignty over both the Asuras and the Suras belongs to me today.
The Great Kaula, the great knowledge, the definitive teaching of Kulakaula, which [destroys] the dense thicket of the delusive cycle of existence and the darkness of the veil of ignorance. (24.2)
Today the snare and net of saṃsāra has been destroyed by you;
today liberation, which is difficult to attain on earth even in its independent state, has been achieved.
Speak again, O Lord of Kaula, concerning the worship of the Siddhas residing within the body.
Bhairava said:
I shall explain that which is doubted; listen to the worship in this Kaula tradition.
The Kula-siddhas, the Yoginīs, and the Rudras [reside] within the Mistress of the Kula (Kulādhipā). 24.4.
O Dear One, all [the deities] belonging to the Goddess are located in the wheel within the heart or even in the head;
one should worship that which is situated externally—this is the procedure for worship, O Beloved. (24.5)
With fragrant *kunda* and *ketakī*, with garlands of jasmine and blue lotuses,
with *campaka* and clusters of *kiṅkara*, and with sweet-smelling blue water lilies.
With various kinds of flowers, including lotuses (*śatapatra*), and substances produced from trees and gathered from the earth, mixed with honey... 24/7.
Flesh, hanging garlands, betel-leaf combined with camphor, the fragrance of incense and sandalwood, aloe-wood, and musk should be offered. (24.8)
Especially with red flowers, it should be well-perfumed with incense and lamps;
one should not offer flowers that are pungent or devoid of fragrance.
External worship has been described; now hear about the internal (ādhyātmika) worship.
All [the deities] wear red garments and are anointed with red perfumes.
The sixteen forms, adorned with such [ornaments],
have serene faces and are drinking the intoxicating liquor.
All of them assume forms at will, are free from old age and death,
are the initiators of creation, and are solely intent upon granting boons.
One should meditate upon [it] beginning with "i"; before long, one shall become equal to that. || 24/12 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Jñānanirṇaya*, brought down by the venerable feet of Matsyendra, the Great Yoginī of the Kaula tradition, and originating from Candradvīpa. || 24/24 ||
The secret word-holding [text] is proclaimed; its definitive conclusion consists of one hundred million verses.
It is the heart-essence of the Siddhas and Yoginīs, most difficult to obtain. (25.1)
O auspicious lady, this which is more secret than the secret, the supreme essence of essences, has been correctly revealed by me, though it is not to be disclosed. 25.2
O Great Goddess, this Mahākaula, consisting of ten hundred [verses], is considered the essence for the determination of knowledge; it is known by the name Sāhasrika. (25.3)
Thus ends the *Sāra* (Essence), brought down by the venerable feet of Matsyendra, within the *Mahākaula-jñānanirṇaya*.
